articles.title: Fluoride in Pregnancy Tied to Lower Problem-Solving Scores, Study Finds
articles.content:
Children exposed to fluoride in the womb at levels meeting the federal safety threshold scored measurably lower on tests of memory and problem-solving, according to a study of more than 2,500 U.S. children.

When mothers’ neighborhood water supply reached around or above this level, each additional increase of 0.5 mg/L was associated with a nearly 3.5-point drop in children’s problem-solving scores.

To give the numbers some context, 0.675 mg is lower than the U.S. Public Health Service’s current recommendation of 0.7 milligrams of fluoride per liter.

The study found the strongest effect in children under age 7.

Declines in Problem Solving

Researchers tracked children born between 2006 and 2019, testing their cognitive abilities between ages 3 and 17. To estimate each child’s fluoride exposure before birth, the team matched fluoride measurements from local water systems to the addresses where mothers lived during pregnancy.

The study found a link between fluoride exposure and fluid cognition: the ability to solve new problems, retain short-term information, and adapt. It did not find a link between fluoride and “crystallized cognition”—skills such as vocabulary and general knowledge that are typically built up through education and experience.

Fluoride is added to water to prevent tooth decay and protect enamel. Though fluoride is also added to toothpastes and mouthwash, these products are only meant to sit on the tooth surface and be spit out, while water fluoridation is ingested and absorbed, Dr. Kevin Khachatryan, co-Founder and dentist at the Empower Dental Group in California, and not involved in the study, told The Epoch Times.

Regulation Battles

The study arrives in the middle of a fast-moving political and legal battle over fluoride’s future in U.S. drinking water.

In September 2024, Senior Judge Edward Chen of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California ruled that current fluoride levels of 700 mg/L already pose an unreasonable risk to children’s neurodevelopment and asked the EPA to review the evidence to see whether the current fluoride recommendations should be altered.

The level at which Chen ruled required further review was far lower than EPA’s upper limit of 4.0 mg/L. EPA has since appealed Chen’s decision.

Although EPA has successfully appealed the decision to conduct a fluoride safety evaluation in court, it will still have to do the review because of HHS administrative orders.

Dentists not involved in the study urged caution on both sides of the debate. Every public health decision will have its risks and benefits, and decisions in dentistry are no exception, Dr. Steve Mascarin, a dentist and CEO of Eleven Dental in Toronto, who was not involved in the study, told The Epoch Times. For this reason, he said, “We must be sure to recognize the cumulative research that supports this position.”

“However, we must also remain open to further research on this topic to inform our practice as science is still capable of evolving our understanding of fluoride,” he said.

Dr. Michael J. Wei, a cosmetic and restorative dentist in Manhattan, echoed that the new findings deserve attention without overstatement: “This study raises important questions about prenatal fluoride exposure and contributes valuable data to an ongoing area of research.”

For now, the study’s authors said the priority is more research. They’re calling for further work to identify exactly when during pregnancy or childhood fluoride exposure matters most, and how to weigh any developmental risks against fluoride’s well-documented benefits for preventing tooth decay.

articles.title: Infant Bleeding Incidents Rise Alongside Vitamin K Shot Refusals: Studies
articles.content:
More bleeding episodes in infants have been recorded as parents increasingly refuse to have vitamin K injections administered, a pair of studies found.

“Routine intramuscular vitamin K administration has been highly effective at preventing vitamin K deficiency bleeding in newborns for decades,” Dr. Heather H. Burris, one of the study’s co-authors and a neonatologist at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, said in a statement.

“Our study is the first to document a nationwide decline in administration paired with increases in bleeding risks. Our findings underscore the importance of continued education and awareness, so families understand the serious, preventable bleeding risks for infants who do not receive vitamin K at birth.”

A minority of the infants diagnosed with the conditions received vitamin K, the researchers said.

“We should continue to follow these trends moving forward since the rates of vitamin K deficiency and vitamin-K-deficient bleeding may continue to rise if vitamin K refusal keeps increasing,” Dr. Elizabeth Wolf, a pediatrician at the Children’s Hospital of Richmond at Virginia Commonwealth University and one of the authors of the study, said in a statement. “We need to better understand why parents are refusing vitamin K and what can be done to improve the uptake of this important medication.”

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend all babies receive a vitamin K shot at birth.

Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in infants can cause bruising, especially around the head and face, or bleeding from the nose or umbilical cord, as well as in areas such as the brain, according to the CDC. Symptoms can include pale skin or gums, yellowish eyes, bloody stool, vomiting, irritability, seizures, or excessive sleepiness.

Loss of Trust?

Dr. Joel Warsh, a pediatrician in California who was not involved with the new papers, told The Epoch Times in an email that he generally recommends vitamin K shots for newborns because evidence shows those who do not receive one face a greater risk of serious bleeding.

“I think the much bigger story here is the growing lack of trust in medicine. Over the past several years, especially during COVID, so many parents have felt pressured, dismissed, or forced into medical decisions,” Warsh said. “Whether everyone agrees with those feelings or not, they are real, and the consequences are becoming increasingly obvious. Many parents no longer trust pharmaceutical companies, public health agencies, or even their own doctors. And that distrust doesn’t necessarily stop at vaccines. It can extend to almost any medical intervention, including something as longstanding as newborn vitamin K.”

Warsh said the solution is having honest conversations with parents about the risks and benefits of medical interventions.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, the CDC’s parent agency, told The Epoch Times via email that the vitamin K injection should be given within six hours of birth to prevent bleeding.

“Uptake of the birth dose has declined in recent years as public trust in healthcare institutions has fallen, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic amid heavy-handed mandates and inconsistent messaging during the Biden administration,” the spokesperson said. “Rebuilding that trust requires honesty, informed consent, and respect for individual choice.”

More on New Papers

The new papers were published by the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) and JAMA Pediatrics.

In the one co-authored by Burris, the researchers looked at data from Epic Systems Corporation’s Cosmos platform, which contains patient records from more than 2,000 hospitals and 49,000 clinics across all 50 states. The researchers noted that not receiving the vitamin K shot was associated with higher rates of bleeding, but that instances also increased among infants who did receive the shot.

“While reasons for this trend are unclear, it could reflect increased ascertainment or sicker maternal-infant dyads,” they wrote. “Interestingly, bleeding risk has risen faster among infants with vitamin K nonreceipt, suggesting that ascertainment, co-occurring pathology, or treatment patterns may differ by vitamin K receipt. While studies to disentangle differential temporal trends may be warranted, there remains a strong association between nonreceipt of vitamin K and bleeding.”

Limitations included the study excluding infants born at less than 35 weeks gestation.

Conflicts of interest included one of the researchers receiving grants from Pfizer, which manufactures a vitamin K shot. Funding came from the National Institutes of Health.

The other set of researchers also used Cosmos and excluded infants born at less than 35 weeks of gestation. They identified the share of newborns receiving a vitamin K injection dropping from 97.7 percent to 95 percent between 2017 and 2025. According to this study, about 60 percent of infants diagnosed with vitamin K deficiency and 81 percent of those diagnosed with vitamin K deficiency bleeding had not received a shot of vitamin K.

“Although association does not prove causality, the data raise concerns about increased parental rejection of vitamin K injections and potential harm to infants,” the researchers said.

Funding came from the Children’s Hospital Foundation, associated with the Children’s Hospital of Richmond. No conflicts of interest were reported.

articles.title: Japan Announces Emergency Cybersecurity Package Following a Wave of Attacks
articles.content:
Japan on Friday announced an emergency cybersecurity package that includes the use of artificial intelligence and cyber rescue teams after a wave of massive data breaches hit major companies and government agencies.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told a ministerial meeting Friday that a rapid response to potential attacks is essential in the era of AI-generated attacks. She urged both government agencies and companies to step up their preparedness.

The emergency package comes after dozens of companies and government agencies were hit by unauthorized access to their systems and leaks of client data, prompting uneasiness across Japan.

“At this very moment, cases of unauthorized access and data breaches are occurring, causing a major impact on daily lives of the people and corporate activities,” Takaichi said. “Let us increase the response capability across Japan by devoting all government resources.”

Measures in the 10 billion yen ($63 million) package are designed to build a resilient society in which the public and private sectors share information, provide swift assistance to the affected and recover from damage.

It aims to acquire one of the world’s highest levels of cybersecurity.

The government will enhance its capability to access servers used by hackers as a preemptive measure known as “active cyber defense,” which was legalized in October.

In case of a possible challenge to Japan’s national security, the government will deploy a support team of officials from the Defense Ministry, the National Police Agency and the National Cybersecurity Office.

Under the measures in the package, a “top gun” team of cybersecurity experts will be set up by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry by the end of November. Team members will use AI to counter hackers and detect weaknesses in network systems. They are to cooperate with technology companies and advanced AI developers of friendly nations to keep Japan’s security expertise up to date.

There will also be a “cyber rescue team” of experts from the public and private sectors to provide initial responses to companies affected by cyberattacks. A separate team will help vulnerable companies to strengthen their defenses.

articles.title: Medical kidnapping: Who protects families from the system?
articles.content:
Podcast: Play in new window | Download | Embed

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | RSS

A parent asking for a second medical opinion should not have to wonder whether that question will cost them their child. When government turns a treatment disagreement into an accusation of abuse, every American family has reason to pay attention.

That is the danger behind what critics call medical kidnapping: children removed from parents who dispute a recommended treatment or whose children have medical conditions mistaken for abuse. The damage reaches beyond a courtroom. A frightened child loses the comfort of home, and parents face a system with enormous power over their future.

Spike Cohen, founder of You Are the Power, argues that funding incentives help drive wrongful removals and prolonged foster placements. His organization works to reunite families and change the laws that allow these cases to continue. His warning deserves attention: agencies cannot be trusted simply because their mission sounds compassionate.

Children facing genuine abuse need protection. Emergency intervention can be necessary. Government must then promptly demonstrate why a child cannot safely return home. Parents deserve meaningful due process, access to medical records, and a fair opportunity to present independent medical evidence.

Informed consent must mean something, too. Doctors should explain risks, benefits, and alternatives. Parents should be able to ask questions without having their concern treated as proof of neglect.

This problem does not stop at a Republican or Democratic state line. Neither will its solution come simply from electing another politician who promises to fix everything.

Start with the families already caught in the machinery. Bring their stories into public view. Demand accountability from the officials making these decisions. Turn that attention into lasting legal safeguards.

The answer is greater freedom, informed consent, and real limits on government power. Families should make medical choices with their doctors, without the threat of losing their children for asking questions.

It’s 6 Eastern. It’s 3 o’clock Pacific. We will draw this city closer together. Coast to coast and around the world from the America Out Loud Talk Radio Studios.

We will replace the frigidity of rugged individualism with the warmth of collectivism. It’s time for The Truth Be Told with Booker Scott. There are so many problems in this nation and this world. Do we need another one to worry about?

Well, I think we should at least dig into it and find out what medical kidnapping is all about. It’s gone on for years, and you may not know anything about it. And that’s what we’re going to do tonight is help you understand this problem that’s happening right here in America. It’s called medical kidnapping.

And Google searches for those two words. They have spiked 300% since 2023. So a lot of people are finding out about it, and a lot of people are learning about it. That’s what we’re going to do here in this hour.

I’m Booker Scott, and this is The Truth Be Told on America Outlaw Talk Radio. Thank you so much for joining us live tonight. Or if you found us later on the podcast, thank you for doing that. Joining the program tonight will be Dr. Irene Avercock, as she has been on this program a couple of times.

She’s a friend of mine, a colleague in freedom and liberty for this nation. She is also vaccine injured. That happened to her in 2012. Since then, a big part of her medical practice has been helping those who are vaccine injured.

She’s been a busy person since 2020, and the vaccine started for COVID. Dr. Irene Mavakakis, thank you for joining us here on this program. Well, thank you, Booker. And it’s just been wonderful getting to know you and becoming friends and colleagues in Liberty.

I really appreciate doing these spaces with you. And I look forward to a great discussion on medical freedom, informed consent, definitions of medical neglect, and what mandatory reporters are. And super excited as you introduce Spike Cohen, who’s another friend and colleague in Liberty. Yeah.

Liberty and freedom. It seems like when it comes to medical advice, we all should have that. We go into a doctor’s office and there’s the white coat. And I have friends and family members, their blood pressure goes up when they see the white coat.

We should have that respect for that doctor, but not over asking questions and having them legitimately answer them for us. And sometimes I don’t know that they are capable of actually answering the questions that we ask. And that’s what comes into informed consent. And we’re going to get into that here on this program.

I want to introduce the next guest. His name is Spike Cohen. Spike is the founder of You Are the Power. It’s a nonprofit, but before that, in 2020, he was the vice presidential nominee for the Libertarian Party.

He was on that ticket in 2020. Spike, it’s great to have you. Welcome to the program. Thank you, Booker.

It’s great to be on. And yeah, at You Are the Power. We protect people against abuse of local governments, and we fight to ensure not only that the abuse stops happening to those families and those individuals, but also that we ensure changes that ensure that that abuse never happens again. And that can look like keeping people from losing their homes to eminent domain, fighting to get bogus charges dropped against people, getting corrupt officials to either change their ways or resign in disgrace.

And relevant to what we’re talking about today, it increasingly it also looks like us reuniting families who where parents were wrongfully accused of abuse. Their children were essentially stolen from them in order to be trafficked. And the reason that I use the term trafficked is because their funding, both federally and state, is tied to how many people they accuse of abuse, how many children they take, how long those children are put in foster care, and a bunch of other perverse incentive structures that encourage them to take children at scale, knowing very often that there’s no good reason for them to be doing it. We’ve successfully reunited multiple families.

We’ve gotten legislation passed in Georgia, a bill called Ridges Law, and which which helps to make it a lot harder for them to do that. And we are working on getting similar legislation passed in in multiple states across the country. And we are in the meantime, we are continuing to find families that have had this happen to them and to reunite them as we’ve already done for so many others. Well, thank you for that great work, and let’s talk about something specifically as we start off here.

Let’s talk about medical kidnapping. Someone may hear that and wonder what in the world is that about? Please explain that to the audience and then what happens from there. And I believe that brings in your work and what you’re trying to do and reunite people.

But let’s talk about medical kidnapping. Yeah, broadly speaking, when I use the term medical kidnapping, I’m referring to the use of the medical system via the state to seize children from parents who have done nothing wrong. And that can broadly be put into two different categories. One of them is where a hospital system or a doctor will recommend a certain treatment or course of treatment or vaccination or something like that, and the some medical recommendation of some kind for a child, and the parent will say, No, I would like a second opinion.

And instead of not acting like a psychopath and allowing the parents to make decisions for their children, they accuse them of neglect and abuse, they bring the state in, they take their kids, and and and say, well, we’re we’re saving the lives of these children by taking them from their evil parents who wanted a second opinion. And very often these things are tied to drugs that have black box warnings, all sorts of of scary things that the parents at the very least have the right to make that that that other opinion or to get another opinion. The other form, and I I consider this a type of medical kidnapping as well, is when a child has injuries that are completely explained by a chronic health condition they have. So Ellers-Danlow syndrome, metabolic bone disorder, osteogenesis imperfecta, complications from the birth during the the actual process of the birth or things that they went through during gestation.

There’s a medical explanation for the injuries that they have. Those medical explanations are intentionally ignored by both the medical establishment and the and the the child protective agencies, and they basically pretend that the children were abused and that that’s what caused the injuries. They do this despite actual diagnoses from medical experts who don’t get their funding from taking children. The family court judges are on all of these cases and on it because that’s how they get their funding as well.

And like I said, it’s it in both cases, it is a type of child trafficking. It is the taking of children from innocent parents to give to another family with a financial incentive built in. I was gonna ask where these children go, but I think you just answered it. They go to another family.

How is that family chosen? Are they just are adopting children? What what does the state do with those children when they take them? Well, it depends on the state.

Usually they go into the foster care system and very often they go for quite some time because that’s how that’s part of how they get their money. The longer the children can be in the foster care system, the more money they get, which is why they’re going for the youngest children possible. So, if you have a very young child who weeks old, sometimes days old, is already showing signs of neonatal rickets or, like I said, complications from the actual birthing process, all of which has either been documented or will soon be documented once the actual injuries are discovered. That’s like the prime thing for them because they could be in the foster care system for a decade or longer.

And the idea eventually is once the parental rights have truly been terminated, then they can be placed for adoption. But that doesn’t mean that they immediately go to a family. There’s a lot of red tape there. So what ends up happening is they’re in whatever the foster care system looks like in that state.

Some states are worse than others. In Georgia, they’ve lost 2,000 children in in just just since 2020. And the the reason is they just don’t have enough foster families. And so the kids go into all sorts of all sorts of situations.

They go into if they’re old enough, quote unquote, old enough, if they’re in their teens, they’ll often just put them in hotel rooms, which is nuts. They’ll often have them in if they’re adolescents, they’ll often have them sleeping in the the offices of the CPS workers. The in New Hampshire, they’ve built what is essentially a prison, which is called the Sununu Youth Center, where children as young as six, again, these are children that have done nothing wrong. They are the the state actually believes that they have been abused.

So not only have they done nothing wrong, they they consider them victims of abuse, they put them in a prison with juvenile offenders, and I I I don’t have to tell you what happens to the in a in a situation like that. But that it’s so it really depends on the state, on how just how at scale they are taking children to the point where they really have nowhere to put them. In some cases, they’re literally building prisons to put them in there. Coming or I’m sorry, youth centers that are part of a a prison.

Okay, coming through 2020 and COVID and the 21, we had medical tyranny in a lot of ways when it came to the vaccine. And that’s what you’re talking about here on one side of it, before you get to the injuries that may have occurred, that they do not think they being in the medical professionals do not believe happened naturally because they have a disease or some other reason. But let’s get to the medical tyranny part of it, because you have some states I would assume that are worse than others. And if you do not follow, I’m assuming, the vaccine schedule, as the state put out, and you question it, and you mentioned that if you just say I want a second opinion, then they can put you on their that list and your child is going to be taken from you.

Is that what you’re saying? Absolutely, and I Irene can definitely get more deeply into the vaccine end of it, but that’s true as well. We’ve had parents who had chosen not to have their children vaccinated for certain things, and when they’re when their kids were seized, they received every vaccine. We actually had a this isn’t specific to vaccines, but it is to medical second opinion.

So we had a a mother in Texas who took her, I forget how old, but it was a matter of months old child to a doctor because he was showing signs of of an infection. And the doctor recommended, I forget the name of it, but it was a it was an antibiotic that when she looked it up on her phone, it said, do not give to children under 12, I think, or something like that. No, he was nowhere near the age and had a black box warning. And so she got a second opinion, and they said, Yeah, there we would never give a child that that drug.

We’ll we’ll put him on whatever the recommended antibiotic was. And so they did that. But while that was happening, the other doctor had the police or had CPS there in Texas seize her child. The child was put under the care of the hospital system of this of under this doctor’s care.

He had the child given that that drug, and the child almost died until they finally started having strokes and and seizures and all sorts of things, and and they had to take the child off of that drug, and lo and behold, the child was okay again. And so that was a case where the mother was it was a doctor that was being that was engaging in malpractice by recommending that drug in the first place. But because he’s the doctor, he’s tied in with that so-called child protective system, he was able to have the child taken from her. And she we are still fighting to help her get that that kid back.

Yeah. So it it’s not about politics, is it? Because you have talked about Texas, you’ve talked about Georgia, and a lot of people would think that maybe a blue state would be, more tyrannical when it came to vaccines. But let’s talk about vaccines real quick.

Let’s get Dr. Irene Maverkakis in here. Let’s talk about vaccines on the schedule and and what you see as a doctor when this happens to these kids in medical kidnapping. Well, thank you, Booker. And I think it’s important to discuss what is the context of this.

The context of this is the concept of what is medical neglect, and there’s both the general definition of medical neglect, and then there’s the legal definitions in each state, and then the concept of mandatory reporting, and then more importantly, what is informed consent, right? So government doctors and healthcare providers, their duty is to protect life and they work for us. And in these United States, we have a right to informed consent, which is the free ability decline, and without that declination being tied to life, liberty, property, and the pursuit of happiness and taking your kid away by all means is infringement upon your civil liberties. So the concept of mandatory reporting, a lot of us, including me in my own state as a physician, we are mandatory reporters, and so are a lot of teachers and healthcare providers, and and what does that mean?

So it means that if we have a reasonable degree of suspicion that some abuse is happening, we are required to report and it’s tied to fines and licensure for us. So, what is the spirit and letter of that in Delaware, for example? So, real quick, let me interrupt you, Irene. I I’m sorry.

I want people to understand that you could lose your license and your livelihood if you do not report something that you see as abuse or if they are not taking a vaccine that is on the schedule. You could literally lose your livelihood over this, couldn’t you? Well, A, I don’t give vaccines because that’s not part of my specialty. And given a vaccine that can be used, someone refusing a vaccine that is on the vaccine schedule has been in some states in some places used as the beginning to open up a CPA CPS case by a physician who had the view that vaccines are 100% safe and effective, which is not true, and that if you refuse, you should be reported to CPS.

So those cases have happened, but I don’t have specific details about those cases. So that is something that has happened. Now, this mandatory reporting, every two years I have to take one hour CME. Most doctors have to take one hour CME.

In order to renew your license, you cannot actually go to renew unless you take this mandatory course. And I just want people to understand the difference between what we’re talking about, medical kidnapping, and the spirit and letter of these mandatory reporting and neglect. The reason why Delaware had a law put in about 10 years ago was because there was a physician in Delaware, Dr. Bradley, who for decades was taking children who were coming to his practice to see him into his basement and sexually abusing them and videotaping them. And the idea that all those people in and out of that office didn’t know that that was going on, he is in jail.

And what he would do is they would schedule never do this. And it’s a little bit of a digression, but it’s really important. He would schedule like a young mom who’s has three young kids and the dad’s working, and they give them all the same appointment and tell them they had to be in different rooms. Very weird, but that was the way that he got access to them.

That is the context of this various sorts of mandatory reporting. And there are instances of kids being abused in different situations, but we have to bear on the side of the concept that we have to allow patients and parents to have informed consent. So when you go to the doctor with your child and they say this is a drug I recommend to your child, the and these are the risks and benefits, but I would tell you that almost all the time in these United States, there’s no informed consent for vaccines and there’s no informed consent for a lot of medications. But if we pretend that they actually tried to give informed consent and you chose to decline, that is your right as the protector of the bodily autonomy of your child, which is so far different from literally it’s obvious that the child is getting beaten at home and has evidence of malnutrition and things like that.

Now, there’s mistakes that happen all the time, and Spike will give you those examples. The kid with the multiple broken bones, if the doctor doesn’t bother to run the differential diagnosis and see that the reason why the kid has broken bones is because they have a medical condition that gives them brittle bone disease. And that’s a big crux of the problem, is oftentimes doctors are not looking at the more unusual and less common medical conditions that lead to things that can mimic or present themselves as abuse. And some of those cases include some of those shaken baby kids, where the parents, when you watch the court cases, you’re like, there’s no way that parent, shook that baby and killed that kid, because you’re if you just deal with people, and some of those were vaccine injuries.

If you go back and look at some of the data, there was high levels of histamine in the brain related to allergic reactions. There were really SIDS deaths, all those kinds of things. And so it’s a very, very, very important line that we have to draw. There’s a big difference between medical neglect, and there is a mandatory reporting requirement, but informed consent, an individual bodily autonomy, and the parent is the protector of that child, has to take precedence.

Spike, I want to come back to you real quick. You were talking about missing children, 2,000 this year. How many missing children do you think there are in this country as a result of medical kidnapping? I mean, we already know it’s in the thousands just in Georgia alone.

So it’s it would be not remotely unreasonable to think that it could be in the tens of thousands across the country, if not the hundreds of thousands. And when I say missing, very often a lot of these kids that that that go missing are are adolescents and teens. A lot of them are probably being trafficked. I mean, after all, they were living in hotel rooms and often in the same, a whole block of rooms on a hotel with a bunch of other teenagers.

Now, if you’re looking for kids and teens to traffic, I mean, you just hit a cornucopia there, right? And it’s and in fact, there was actually a situation in New Hampshire where they were catching actual abuse happening, where officials were looking the other way. And and there’s if I recall, there were even allegations that that they were actually being paid to give them access to these kids. But I mean, no, it’s it’s it’s the most horrific things that you can think about that are happening in these scenarios, and things I don’t even want to repeat.

But yeah, no, I mean there’s there’s many of them that are missing. And and I will say, and this is certainly not in their defense, but putting some more context in it, a lot of them just aged out. A lot of them are just over the age of 18 now, and there’s no reason for them to report. And we don’t know what happened.

They might have just gone home to their families. Once they’re past a certain age, they don’t have to keep track of them anymore. So you picture a situation where you’re wrongfully accused of abuse, your 14-year-old is taken from you, you’re not allowed to speak with them or have any communications with them, they’re living in a hotel room, and around the age of 18, they just leave and come home or go to another family member, or God forbid, go off and do their own thing, and you don’t even know where they are. I mean, these are these are horrific things that are happening under the umbrella or the veil of so-called child protection, and it’s no, it is no such thing.

Now, some of these kids have actually legitimately been abused, and they’re also going through this. So it’s it’s just it’s a terrible thing all around. It is it is what happens, and this is my, going back to my libertarian warning about government in general. This is the things that happen when we put government in charge of something that’s very important.

They create weird incentive structures that often make the problem worse, or at the very least, don’t improve it. They often create other ancillary problems related to that thing and actually worsen the issue. And and then every year they go, well, yeah, the problem’s gotten worse. So we need more money.

And so it becomes costly. And and by doing in doing so, they they they rob us of the ability to really seek better alternatives. There’s a way to protect children, and and this is not it. articles.title: Strategies to scale your MSSP without adding headcount
articles.content:
For many MSSPs, it's a challenge to build businesses that can handle more customers, deliver better security and generate more revenue without adding employees at the same pace.

It's a hot topic in the industry and a major focus of MSSP Alert Live 2026, a free virtual event taking place Nov. 17-18. Throughout the two-day online conference, industry leaders will share practical strategies for breaking the cycle of hiring to meet demand and build more profitable security businesses.

To get some additional perspective in preparation for the event, we spoke with previous MSSP Alert Top 250 honoree PDI Technologies and its Senior VP and GM of Security & Network Solutions, Ameer Karim.

Revenue is growing. But is your business getting healthier?

For MSSPs, growth can be a double-edged sword. More customers bring more revenue, but they also bring more endpoints to protect, more alerts to investigate and more pressure on security teams.
That's why Karim believes MSSPs need to think about scalability long before they reach capacity.

"Because our customers at PDI are large organizations with many distributed locations, we design for scale from the start," Karim said. "Our solutions are built to onboard and support thousands of new locations quickly, without affecting the tens of thousands that already depend on us."

But supporting more customers is only part of the equation. MSSPs also need to make sure growth isn't coming at the expense of service quality.

It's entirely possible for revenue to climb while response times get longer, analysts become overwhelmed and customers grow less satisfied. On paper, the business looks successful. Behind the scenes, the cracks will start to show.

Karim recommends looking beyond revenue and focusing on three indicators of sustainable growth: service delivery KPIs and their trends, continued investment in research and development, and customer outcomes such as retention.
"Too many MSSPs skip past these and measure health by revenue growth instead, but revenue is a lagging indicator because it can keep climbing while service quality slips and capabilities fall behind," he said.

The takeaway for MSSP leaders is simple: Growth isn't just about how many new customers you can bring in. It's about how well you can support them, keep existing customers happy and continue improving your services without overwhelming your team.

Stop hiring your way around broken processes

As an MSSP grows, so does the workload. More clients mean more security alerts, more investigations and more demands on technical staff. Eventually, hiring additional analysts or engineers can seem like the only way to keep up.

But before adding headcount, MSSPs should take a closer look at what is slowing down output.

"Avoiding bottlenecks starts with planning, standardization, and automation, not simply adding resources," Karim said.

At PDI, that means building services that can support thousands of additional customer locations without disrupting existing operations. Rather than relying on employees to handle every new requirement, the company focuses on creating processes and systems that can adapt as demand increases.

"A next-generation MSSP is built so that when a known condition occurs, the service already knows how to adapt," Karim said.

For other MSSPs, there are opportunities to apply the same thinking to everyday operations. Customer onboarding, routine investigations, configuration changes and responses to common security events are all areas where standardized workflows and automation can reduce manual effort.

The key is identifying which activities genuinely require human expertise and which can be handled more efficiently through technology and established processes.

Hiring will always be part of growing a security business. But MSSPs that address operational inefficiencies before expanding their teams will be in a better position to control costs, maintain service quality and support more customers without a corresponding increase in headcount.

Let AI do the heavy lifting, not the thinking

AI and automation can help MSSPs support more customers without adding headcount. But automating more tasks doesn't automatically translate into better security or greater efficiency. At PDI, automation helps threat hunters identify critical events faster, SOC analysts investigate and respond more efficiently and engineers improve detection performance.

"We use automation and AI to strengthen our experts, not replace them. It handles the work that slows experts down, so they can focus on the judgment calls automation can't make," Karim said.

But automation can become a liability when it applies the same rules and responses to every customer. Karim points to PDI's experience protecting fuel stations and automotive dealerships.

"Heavy network traffic at 2 a.m. is normal for a station that never closes. At a dealership that locked its doors hours earlier, it's a red flag," he said. "If your automation can't tell the difference, you're relying on it too much."

MSSPs need automated workflows that account for customer-specific operating hours, network behavior and business risks. Standardization supports scalability, but it shouldn't compromise threat detection.

They should also track whether automation is improving response times, reducing unnecessary escalations and increasing analyst capacity without sacrificing service quality.

The goal isn't to eliminate human involvement. It's to make better use of human expertise while creating room to grow.

The next generation of MSSPs will be built differently

As AI becomes standard in managed security, simply adopting the technology won't be enough to stand out. The competitive advantage will come from how effectively MSSPs use it to improve efficiency, service quality and profitability.

"The winners will be the ones that designed their services around it from day one, not the ones bolting it onto processes built around headcount," Karim said.

For new MSSPs, that means building scalability into their services from the start, with automated workflows and repeatable processes that can accommodate growth without continually adding staff. For established MSSPs, the challenge is identifying inefficient workflows, automating repetitive tasks and modernizing services that depend on manual effort.

In either case, the goal is the same: Build a business where revenue can grow faster than staffing costs without sacrificing the quality of protection customers expect.

Sometimes the best way to move forward is to step away

Running an MSSP doesn't leave much time to think about the bigger picture. Between supporting customers, responding to threats, managing employees and growing the business, it's easy to get caught up in day-to-day operations.

"Running an MSSP keeps you in the weeds, so events like MSSP Alert Live are one of the few chances to step back, look at the bigger picture, and see where best practices are heading, how customer expectations are changing, and where the industry is moving," he said.

Of course, growing an MSSP will sometimes require hiring more people. Running a lean operation is one thing, but stretching employees too thin can compromise service quality, increase burnout and create security risks.

The goal isn't to build the smallest possible team. It's to build a business where people, processes and technology work together to support sustainable growth. MSSPs that get that balance right will grow their revenue for years to come.

Learn more at MSSP Alert Live

Want to learn how leading MSSPs are using AI, automation and advanced security services to reduce customer risk and drive profitable growth? Join us for MSSP Alert Live, Nov. 17–18, a free virtual conference featuring practical strategies for scaling security operations and expanding services.

articles.title: Why You Should Cook and Chill Potatoes Before Mashing
articles.content:
Mashed potatoes and gravy go hand-in-hand with dishes like Thanksgiving turkey, chicken-fried steak, and meatloaf. However, sometimes you want mashed potatoes and gravy when you don’t have pan drippings.

After dental work a few years ago, I was hungry and tired of liquids, but I needed a soft, comforting meal. For some reason, in the middle of summer, I started craving mashed potatoes and gravy, so my husband made them for me. With no meat cooking and no pan drippings to work with, he made delicious, umami-rich gravy using a few simple ingredients.

I’ve mastered making flavorful pan drippings for gravy. I’ll show you how to make rich poultry or beef gravy, with or without pan drippings, and share a simple make-ahead mashed potato technique that may benefit blood sugar and gut health.

The Best Drippings for Gravy

One Thanksgiving, my husband and I each prepared a turkey and made separate batches of gravy. Mine won our family taste test. Here’s what I did:

I arranged a sliced onion, two celery ribs, two carrots, and a few sprigs of fresh sage, thyme, and rosemary around the turkey in the roasting pan. Then I poured 1 cup of broth over the top, followed by 1/2 cup of chardonnay. After roasting, I strained the drippings and used the liquid for the gravy.

For Beef Roast Gravy:Follow the same method using thyme or your favorite herbs, beef broth, and dry red wine.

Note:Most, but not all, of the

alcoholcooks off.

For an Alcohol-Free Version:Simply omit the wine. The meat, vegetables, herbs, and broth will still produce flavorful drippings for gravy.

Why Cook and Chill Potatoes Before Mashing?

Researchsuggests that cooking, chilling, and reheating potatoes may create a more favorable blood-sugar and insulin response after eating, although results vary depending on how you prepare the potatoes.

This recipe includes a chilling step for both health benefits and make-ahead convenience, so you only have to reheat and mash the potatoes at dinner time. Because reheating can reduce some of the resistant starch created during chilling, rewarm them gently rather than getting them piping hot.

Mashed Potatoes and Gravy

Make creamy mashed potatoes and savory gluten-free gravy with pan drippings when you have them—or without when you don’t.

Prep Time:20 minutes

Cook Time:35 minutes

Total Time:4 hours

Servings:6

Ingredients

  • 2 1/2 pounds Russet or Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 2-inch chunks

  • 2 teaspoons sea salt, divided

  • 2 tablespoons ghee, butter, or olive oil

  • 3 tablespoons organic cornstarch

  • 3 tablespoons filtered water

  • 1 tablespoon collagen peptides (optional)

  • Strained pan drippings (however much you have)

  • Chicken or beef bone broth, as needed to make 2 cups with the drippings

  • 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

  • 1 teaspoon mushroom powder (ground from dried mushrooms; optional, for savory depth)

  • 1/2 teaspoon sea salt

  • 1/4 teaspoon garlic powder

  • 2 cups chicken or beef bone broth

Instructions

Step 1:Place the potatoes in a large pot and cover with cold water by about 1 inch. Add 1 teaspoon salt. Cover and bring to a gentle boil over medium-high heat. Uncover and reduce the heat as needed to maintain a gentle simmer. Cook about 20 minutes until fork-tender.

Step 2:Drain the potatoes well, reserving the potato water. Refrigerate the potato water. Spread the potatoes on a baking sheet; refrigerate once they stop steaming. Chill at least four hours or overnight.

Step 3:When ready to mash, reheat the reserved potato water in a small saucepan and keep warm. Place the potatoes, ghee, butter or olive oil, remaining 1 teaspoon salt, and 1/4 cup warm potato water in a larger saucepan over low heat. Cover and heat, stirring occasionally, until warm throughout.

Step 4:Mash with a masher or ricer, adding potato water until your preferred texture is reached. Reserve any remaining potato water for the gravy.

Step 5:Cover and keep warm until ready to serve.

Step 6:Whisk the cornstarch and water in a small bowl until smooth. Set aside.

Step 7:Measure the strained pan drippings and add enough broth to equal 2 cups. Warm the drippings and broth in a skillet over medium heat. When the gravy reaches a simmer, whisk the slurry again and slowly pour it into the skillet, whisking constantly.

Step 8:Crumble a few dried mushrooms into a spice grinder or bullet blender and grind until finely powdered. Measure 1 teaspoon; reserve the rest for soups, sauces, or to replace breadcrumbs in meatballs or meatloaf.

Step 9:Heat the olive oil in a skillet over medium-low heat. Stir in the mushroom powder, salt, and garlic powder for 20 to 30 seconds, until fragrant. Add the broth and cook until simmering. Whisk the slurry again and slowly pour it into the skillet, whisking constantly.

Step 10:Simmer either gravy for one to two minutes, whisking, until it thickens and lightly coats the back of a spoon. If too thick, whisk in reserved potato water one tablespoon at a time. Sprinkle the collagen peptides over the top, if using, and stir until fully dissolved.

Step 11:Serve gravy over the potatoes and enjoy.

Storage:Refrigerate leftover mashed potatoes and gravy in separate airtight containers within two hours. Use within three to four days, or freeze for three to four months. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator. Cornstarch-thickened gravy can turn spongy or watery after thawing, so whisk it vigorously. Reheat the potatoes and gravy separately until steaming hot throughout, adding a little water or broth to either one if it has thickened.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Which potatoes are best for mashed potatoes?

A:Russet potatoes have more starch and create a light, fluffy mash. Yukon Golds make a denser, creamier mash with a naturally buttery flavor. Choose your favorite, or a mix of the two.

Q: Can I use a lower-carb vegetable instead of potatoes?

A:Yes. Replace some or all of the potatoes with cooked, mashed cauliflower or celeriac for a lower-carb option. Mashed parsnips are another possibility; they’re only slightly lower in carbs, but have more fiber.

Q: Do I need to use bone broth?

A:No. I use

bone brothfor its rich flavor and amino acids that help support the intestinal lining and gut barrier. Regular broth, stock, or reconstituted powdered bone broth works, too—just check the ingredients.

Q: Why add collagen to gravy?

A:I often sneak collagen peptides into soups, sauces, and hot cereal because they provide

building blocksfor skin, bones, joints, and other connective tissues without changing the flavor or texture. You could even add a tablespoon or two to the hot potatoes when mashing them.

Q: What can I make with leftover mashed potatoes and gravy?

A:Turn leftover mashed potatoes into potato cakes or use them to top shepherd’s pie. Leftover gravy adds flavor and body to soups, pot pie, or hash.

articles.title: Hackers exploit outdated BTCPay Server instances to steal cryptocurrency
articles.content:
Hackers have successfully stolen cryptocurrency from hot wallets hosted on outdated BTCPay Server instances. The breach specifically targeted servers running version 2.4.1 or earlier of the open-source payment platform, according to Infosecurity Magazine.

Blockchain analysis conducted by Bitquery traced approximately $1.63 million in Bitcoin and Litecoin to addresses linked to the thefts. Attackers exploited a vulnerability that was officially patched in version 2.4.2, which was released on August 7. The perpetrators gained administrative access to the servers and performed 682 sweeps of hot wallets between October 30 and November 2. Despite a security warning issued by the project on November 1, 267 additional sweeps occurred after operators were advised to shut down their systems.

Bitquery noted that 87% of the stolen funds were moved in a single wave. BTCPay Server has urged all affected operators to migrate to fresh servers with new wallets and seeds, warning that simply updating the software is insufficient to remove unauthorized access. The project emphasized that wallets with keys held off-server, such as hardware wallets, remain secure. This incident highlights the critical importance of maintaining updated software, as the vulnerability had been known for months before the widespread exploitation began.

Source: Infosecurity Magazine

articles.title: Installing the Fix for an Exploited WordPress Flaw Can Expose Some Sites One Last Time
articles.content:
Some WordPress sites can still be attacked while they install the fix for an actively exploited flaw, according to Umut Bayram, the Picus Security researcher who found it.

The update that installs the fix still unpacks its files using the site's old, unpatched code, so an attacker who strikes at the right moment can run code on the server. The researcher advises blocking web access to the site's wp-content/upgrade folder before updating.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-119977, affects WordPress 4.7 through 7.1.3. During a core update that uses a complete package, WordPress unpacks a copy of the new version into a temporary folder inside wp-content/upgrade. That copy includes the WordPress installer, and the web server can usually reach it.

An attacker with no account who can determine the folder's name and access the installer before WordPress deletes the copy can end up running code on the server. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities earlier this week.

WordPress released the fix last week in version 7.1.4 and in matching updates for older branches back to 4.7, all listed in its security advisory.

The fix gives the temporary folder a random name. But the update that installs the fix unpacks its files using the old code already on the site, as WordPress's updater code shows. On sites running 5.9 or later, that old code names the folder after the downloaded file, so the name can be predicted one last time.

Before the fix, an attacker could use the installer to write a new configuration file, wp-config.php, into the temporary copy. The update would then overwrite the site's real file with that file. The part of the fix that stops this already works during the update that installs it, because WordPress copies the files into place using the new code.

An attacker who catches the window during that update can still set up the temporary copy of WordPress with their own database, log in to it, and run PHP code with the web server's permissions before the copy is deleted, Bayram says in his technical write-up. From there, the attacker can read or write files in the live WordPress site.

Who Is Exposed During the Update

Not every update exposes the installer, the researcher says. Complete packages always include the installer files. A smaller partial package, built for one specific starting version, exposes a site only if it happens to contain them.

On sites that allow automatic background updates, WordPress installs the fix automatically, via the same updater and the same steps.

The Hacker News checked WordPress.org's update service today for several versions. For updates within a branch, such as from 7.1.3 to 7.1.4, it offered a partial package, including for automatic updates. For a move from an older branch, such as from 7.0.7 to 7.1.4, it offered only complete packages.

On 4.4 through 5.8, the old code adds random characters to the folder's name. That hides the name unless the site leaks it some other way, such as in an error message, the researcher says.

Once 7.1.4 or a branch fix is installed, later updates use a random folder name, and a wp-config.php file in the temporary copy is never copied over the real one.

What to Do Before Updating

The researcher's first recommendation is to stop the web server from serving wp-content/upgrade at all. WordPress works with that folder directly on disk, so blocking web access does not break updates, he says.

  • Block the folder in the web server configuration. On Nginx, add location ^~ /wp-content/upgrade/ { deny all; }. On Apache, add Require all denied inside a <Directory> block for that folder in the virtual host configuration.
  • If you can only edit .htaccess, add RedirectMatch 403 ^/wp-content/upgrade/ to the .htaccess file in the WordPress root, above the WordPress rewrite rules.
  • Do not put an .htaccess file inside wp-content/upgrade itself. The old updater deletes everything in that folder before it unpacks an update, so the file would be gone when it is needed.
  • Confirm that a request to /wp-content/upgrade/ returns a 403 error.
  • Update to 7.1.4 or to the fixed release for your branch.

The other safe route, he says, is a manual update done outside the web root, the folder the web server serves. Back up the site files and database, unpack the new release in a folder the web server does not serve, copy the core files into place without touching wp-config.php or wp-content, and then run the WordPress database update. This way, no temporary installer is ever created in a folder the web can reach.

WP-CLI's wp core update command is no substitute, because it runs the same updater and unpacks the package into the same folder.

WordPress 4.6 and earlier no longer receive security updates, so there is no fix for them. The researcher says the flaw goes back to WordPress 2.7, released in 2008, and that those sites should move to a supported version.

Attacks and What to Check

CISA's catalog addition earlier this week was based on evidence of active exploitation, but the agency did not describe the attacks.

Wordfence, the WordPress security company that assigned the CVE identifier, saw attack attempts begin nine minutes after it deployed a firewall rule for the flaw on the day of the release. Two of the busiest sources kept checking small groups of sites for about 14.5 hours, which the company says, in its attack analysis, aligns with attempts to catch the moment a site updates.

Its score for the flaw in the CVE record is 8.1 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. In its lab tests, the window lasted only seconds. WordPress's own advisory rates the flaw low.

Code that its authors describe as an exploit for the flaw has appeared in public GitHub repositories since earlier this week. One of them says its code also works on sites that still use a predictable folder during complete-package updates. Whether the code works has not been established.

For sites that stayed on an affected version after the release, Wordfence suggests looking for:

  • unexpected requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade
  • administrator accounts no one recognizes
  • plugins no one installed
  • PHP files in wp-content/upgrade that no one put there

Update

Bayram told The Hacker News on November 6 that whether a partial update is exposed depends on what that specific package contains. A partial package holds only the files that changed between two releases. If those do not include the installer files, the temporary copy cannot run as a WordPress installation, and the installer never becomes reachable.

A site also does not always get a partial package when one exists. WordPress falls back to a complete package if the site's core files do not match the official checksums or if the update is a reinstall.

The deciding factor, the researcher said, "isn’t partial versus complete. It’s whether the updater already installed on the site has been fixed."

articles.title: Huntress expands automated identity threat protection and security tools
articles.content:
Huntress has expanded its Agentic Security Platform with new automated identity threat protections, managed security information and event management capabilities, and security awareness tools designed to help managed service providers detect and respond to attacks across customer environments, according to coverage from Channel Insider.

The updates include features that use intelligence from confirmed identity attacks to block malicious infrastructure across eligible Microsoft 365 tenants, identify compromised service principals, and investigate 180 days of historical login activity for newly onboarded customers. A new capability in Huntress Managed Identity Threat Detection and Response turns intelligence from confirmed attacks into blocking policies for all eligible tenants.

Additionally, the platform now includes Brute Force Sentry to monitor Windows and Linux environments and Defense Drills, which provide hands-on simulations for users during active compromises. These enhancements aim to reduce manual workloads for managed service providers, who face rising security alert volumes. By automating threat response and providing identity posture assessments, Huntress seeks to help partners manage complex environments more efficiently.

These tools reflect a broader industry shift toward autonomous remediation, allowing providers to offer enterprise-grade protection to small and midsize businesses without the associated complexity. The new capabilities are available to partners as part of the company's ongoing effort to scale threat intelligence and improve security outcomes.

Source: Channel Insider

articles.title: Daniel Flynn and the war on football
articles.content:
Podcast: Play in new window | Download | Embed

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | Podcast Index | RSS

Football season is a good time to reconsider what we have been told about the game. When I interviewed Daniel J. Flynn in April 2023 about The War on Football: Saving America’s Game, I wanted to examine claims that had acquired authority through repetition. His book asks whether the evidence supports the familiar portrayal of football as a route to an early grave.

Flynn is an author and senior editor at The American Spectator; he subsequently became a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution. He approached football through historical research, medical literature, and time spent with teams. The book appeared in 2013, but its historical reach makes it suitable for revisiting well beyond its publication year.

Theodore Roosevelt confronted football’s dangers more than a century ago. As Flynn recounts, the response included changes that helped preserve the game while altering how it was played. Football’s history contains repeated revisions to rules and equipment. Loving the sport has never required preserving every practice that once belonged to it.

Flynn began our conversation with mortality. Reports of famous players’ dying young had encouraged a broader conclusion about the men who played professionally. He asked what happened when researchers counted the entire study population, including the men whose long lives attracted little attention. “Not only did NFL players not die young,” he said, “but they were outliving the general population.”

The federal study found lower overall mortality among its cohort of former NFL players than in the general population. A separate study of suicide mortality also found a lower rate among veteran players. These are aggregate findings with defined populations and comparison groups. They challenge sweeping claims about early death without establishing that every player escapes injury, or that football itself causes longevity.

We also considered what happens when boys lose the opportunity to play. Flynn described the larger boy whose size disadvantages him in some activities but gives him a place on a football team. “I think football is an excellent way to get some of these bigger kids off the couch and into some cleats,” he said. That benefit belongs in an assessment of the sport.

My own son’s experience with football and wrestling gave me reason to recognize that argument. Training required discipline, and different positions rewarded different abilities. The offensive lineman has an assignment to learn; a defensive player must respond as a play develops. A team can make room for boys with different temperaments and physical gifts.

Equipment introduces another question. Could better helmets encourage players to hit harder because they feel protected? That is the possibility of risk compensation, which we explored without claiming to have established its size. Flynn acknowledged that he lacked data on the point and said he preferred modern helmets. Protection and behavior both belong in the inquiry.

Money also shapes the attention a sport receives. I raised the Willie Sutton comparison: the NFL is where the money is. Horseback riding, skiing, and ice hockey expose participants to injury, too, although comparisons depend on the injury and amount of exposure being measured. Football’s wealth creates opportunities for litigation and businesses selling protection.

The streetlight effect describes a related problem: concentrating scrutiny where the subject is most visible. Flynn questioned commercial interests behind concussion products and reporters’ accepting scientific authority without examining those interests. A medical credential does not settle whether a product works. A settlement does not, by itself, measure the population’s risk.

Flynn’s argument includes an ordinary experience that risk calculations can neglect. Boys practice, learn assignments, and return after being knocked down. “I don’t want to say that football is a completely safe game,” he told me. He also asked us to count what the game gives the boys who choose to play it.

Join us at 5 pm ET on weekdays on America Out Loud Talk Radio. Listen on iHeartRadio, our world-class media player, or our free apps on Apple, Android, or Alexa. Discover all the episodes on podcast networks, i.e., Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Pandora, TuneIn, Stitcher, and iHeart. You’ll find them the day after they air on talk radio, available on podcast. Extraordinary voices for extraordinary times.

Transcript Summary of this podcast episode ⤵

Football’s risks are real. So are the costs of frightening boys off the field and onto the couch. A public health argument that counts every collision while ignoring conditioning, discipline, and belonging gives parents an incomplete picture.

The familiar claim that NFL players routinely die young deserves scrutiny. Author Daniel J. Flynn points to a federal mortality study of roughly 3,500 former players that recorded 334 deaths when about 625 were expected. That finding challenges the grim narrative built from famous players’ obituaries.

It does not prove that football makes people live longer. Elite athletes bring unusual physical gifts, exercise habits, financial resources, and access to care. It does mean that a heartbreaking death cannot stand in for the whole population.

For boys, the benefits reach beyond professional ambitions. A larger child who struggles in other sports can find a useful place on the offensive line. Different positions reward different abilities. Coaches establish expectations. Teammates depend on one another. Getting knocked down and choosing to rise can become a lesson that lasts beyond Friday night.

None of this requires pretending concussions are harmless. Keeping a confused, unsteady player off the field is progress. Football has repeatedly changed its rules and equipment to address danger. Preserving the game means continuing that work.

The scrutiny should extend to those selling fear and purported solutions. Scientific credentials do not erase financial interests. Reporters should question concussion products and disclose ownership ties rather than treating a white coat as a guarantee of integrity.

Parents deserve a truthful account of risk, including what children lose when an activity disappears. Sitting still is no refuge from poor health. Life offers no option without danger. Be thoughtful. Be careful. Then leave room for young people to test themselves, find their teammates, and enjoy being alive out in the world.

If we’ve learned anything from these past couple of years, what Americans against that personal medical freedom and liberty are in prices. America Out Loud PULSE brings together the top experts in healthcare-related fields to keep you up beat again. Listen to America Out Loud PULSE Radio on the iHeartRadio Network, and on the America Outload apps for Apple, Android, and Alexa. Don’t miss a moment.

Join us every Friday at 5 p.m. Eastern. I’m Dr. Randall Bock here to unpack myths, explore innovations, and give you actual insights into the world of medicine and health. Football season is well underway, and I’m returning to a conversation with Daniel J. Flynn about his book, The War on Football, Saving America’s Game. We recorded this interview in April 2023, but its subject reaches back more than a century.

Flynn, an author and senior editor at The American Spectator, examines how football became a public health controversy and what the evidence actually says about the men who play it. One hundred years ago and more, Theodore Roosevelt confronted demands to reform or abolish football. He wanted to preserve the game while addressing its dangers. Football has changed repeatedly since then, and Flynn describes the history alongside the more recent claims about shortened lives, concussions, and chronic traumatic encephalopathy, i.e.

Called CTE. One question runs through our conversation. What happens when we count everyone? A famous player’s dying young commands attention.

The men who live into old age seldom receive comparable coverage. Flynn examined mortality studies that included the whole study population, and their findings challenge the familiar account of football players routinely dying before their time. We also consider what boys gain from playing. Football gives a larger boy a place where his size can become advanced an advantage.

It requires conditioning and cooperation, and its different positions reward different abilities. Removing the game means giving up those benefits too. There’s also the aspect that this is a way of channeling aggression. If you have an absence of aggressive sports, you’re not going to take the aggression out of boys and young men.

You’re just going to find other places to do them. I think a really good example is LeBron James, I think we might discuss this later as well, who could have gone one way the way of his father, but he was brought up in a household where there was discipline and I believe a football mentality. And this gave him a structure to take out some of his physical aggressions and so forth. And this is probably true for many other kids across the spectrum, especially in inner city and so forth.

Then there are also the unintended consequences of protection. Could a player’s feeling safer and a better helmet encourage us hitting harder? We explore that possibility along with the financial incentives surrounding the sport. Mind you, horseback riding, ice hockey, and other activities carry risks, but the NFL offers something few sports can match, an enormous pool of money.

Those other ones are probably equally, dangerous for concussions and so forth on a per minute basis of sport played. So this raises questions about where lawyers, businesses, and reporter direct their attention. This is a conference conversation about evidence, incentives, and the experience of playing the game. Here is Daniel Flynn on the war on football.

I’m honored to have one of my favorite authors. I I’ve owned his book for some time, Daniel J. Flynn, the author of The War on Football. This is a book from 10 years ago. But perhaps you can get us up to date.

Tell us a little bit about your theory in the book and about yourself. Hey, it’s great to be here. Yeah, I wrote I wrote the book because I initially wrote an article because there was a lot of chatter in the press from LZ Granderson, from George Will, and from a number of other people that football shortens lives, that people in the NFL, there was a lawsuit, or not a lawsuit, that the NFL Players Association, the union, they had petitioned NIOSH, which is the National Institutes of Occupational Health and Safety, or safety and health, to do a study, a mortality study on whether football players die young. And there was a lot of chatter in the press, like I said, from George Will, from LZ Granderson, from Malcolm Gladwell, from all sorts of people advancing this idea that players in the NFL die at an earlier age.

And there I think the reasoning for this was basically that they would see obituaries of NFL players that would die in their 50s, and they would say, well, this must mean they die young. And not really looking at guys that, lived to an advanced age, like Art Donovan or Frank Gifford or someone like that. So the the federal government looked at about 3,500 NFL players who played from 1959 up until the I think the early 1990s. And they found not only did NFL players not die young, but they were outliving the general population.

They’re expecting to find I think based on that number of players and the age and the averages and all that, they were expecting to find 625 deaths. And what they did find was 334 deaths. And so it was drastically reduced. They were expecting to find an 18% death rate, it was a 10% death rate.

And so when I I wrote an article in The American Spectator basically saying, hey, this isn’t true. Here is the data. There’s a lot of people saying that NFL players die young, but they actually looked at every single NFL player who played, I think it was five or more seasons or four or more seasons, and it showed that if you play football for a long time, you tend to live for a long time. articles.title: Hacker exploits stolen Microsoft Entra ID credentials to target MSPs
articles.content:
A lone hacker is actively exploiting stolen application secrets for Microsoft Entra ID to gain unauthorized access to Microsoft 365 and Azure environments, based on information published by Channeldive.

The attacker targeted 45 application registrations across 18 organizations, successfully authenticating into 33 of them. This breach allowed the actor to compromise 27 organizations, including downstream clients in the energy, government, food and agriculture, transportation and construction sectors. The operator, potentially utilizing a virtual private server in Poland, has accessed 2,300 mailbox items and downloaded 81 files. Approximately 95% of the sign-ins were executed via scripted clients, demonstrating machine-speed activity with rapid bursts of 24 sign-ins within 10 seconds.

Unlike traditional supply chain attacks that rely on compromised software updates, this campaign leverages existing valid secrets for application registrations. Security researchers note that while the cadence suggests the use of automated tooling, there is no direct link to the recent campaign involving the Artex agentic tool. Organizations are advised to monitor for suspicious authentication patterns as the hacking attempts remain ongoing.

Source: Channeldive

articles.title: Hackers Target OpenSSH SSHole Flaw Within Hours of Disclosure, Gain Root on Honeypot
articles.content:
Threat actors are attempting to exploit a recently disclosed security flaw impacting OpenSSH that can enable sign-ins to accounts that have no password set, according to Previdian.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score: 8.1) and codenamed SSHole (or *sshole), impacts Linux systems that run OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled, including Alpine Linux's default OpenSSH server configuration.

An unauthenticated attacker can supply an oversized password to access accounts that are deliberately configured without usable passwords, without having to steal credentials or SSH keys. The issue, discovered by security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, has been addressed in OpenSSH 10.6p2.

The underlying issue dates back to a patch introduced in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210. Under specific conditions, the password-handling behavior in OpenSSH mistakenly interprets a failed password-hashing operation as successful authentication by producing the same value ("*") used to indicate that an account with password disabled at the system level.

An attacker can trigger the vulnerability to authenticate to certain password-disabled accounts using an arbitrary password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long, causing the hash attempt to fail and returning an asterisk. The sshd daemon then compares with the asterisk stored in the account's password field, leading to a successful login.

To be clear, successful exploitation requires at least one account with an asterisk (*) as its password hash. It does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes.

"A successful SSHole attack grants access with the compromised account's existing permissions," Safe Security said. "For enterprise, the consequences of SSHole depend on the privileges of the compromised account."

"While unauthorized SSH access is the immediate impact, attackers may also gain access to deployment credentials, application secrets, and connected infrastructure, potentially enabling lateral movement or service disruption."

It's worth noting that the vulnerability does not affect Dropbear, glibc-based Linux distributions, non-Linux systems, and systems that check passwords through PAM.

Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it observed the first exploitation attempt less than nine hours after the CVE publication, adding it has confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running Alpine Linux and OpenSSH. Telemetry data shows a total of eight exploitation attempts from an IP address geolocated to Japan.

"The observed source IP, 89.116.89[.]18, used oversized passwords to bypass authentication and ran reconnaissance commands including id, uname and hostname through non-interactive SSH sessions," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

Affected users are advised to install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or their distribution's patched package, and then restart sshd. Alpine is also recommending that users investigate "Accepted password for" log entries involving accounts that should not accept password logins.

"Look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password (alpine, root, or any key-only user)," Alpine said. "Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised."

articles.title: Big Tech sues over California plan to limit kids’ scrolling
articles.content:
