articles.title: Microsoft Paint RCE Fix Now Available, but Windows Update Won't Deliver It
articles.content:
A fix for CVE-2026-83844, a remote code execution flaw in Windows Paint, is now in the Microsoft Store. Paint gets this fix only through a Store update, not through Windows updates.

The fixed build, 11.2609.401.0, was the newest Paint build in all ten countries The Hacker News checked today.

The flaw is an out-of-bounds read that could let an attacker run code over a network. Microsoft rates it as Important, with a CVSS score of 8.1, and says that a successful attack requires a deep understanding of the target system. The flaw was not known to be exploited or publicly disclosed when the company published it on October 13.

Brian Vitko of RFF, a device-management software maker, checked which Paint builds the Store offered in six countries earlier this week. He found that the newest in each was 11.2605.81.0, a build without the fix.

His test virtual machine has since moved to the fixed build on its own, through Store auto-update. That is one machine, and how quickly other PCs will get the build is not yet clear.

Which Build Counts as Fixed

Microsoft's security advisory names 11.2609.401.0 as the fixed build. The CVE record for the flaw, which the company also publishes, still lists Paint as affected only below 11.2605.91.0. Its NVD entry shows the same range.

So a scanner that reads the CVE record would treat any build from 11.2605.91.0 up as fixed. A copy at 11.2609.401.0 or later passes under both numbers.

As recently as last week, the advisory gave 11.2605.91.0 as the fixed build, according to a forum question on Microsoft Q&A. The advisory's revision history still shows only its October 13 entry, with no note about the change.

How to Check Every Copy of Paint

Paint, like other Store apps, is installed separately for each user account on a PC. Windows can also keep a provisioned copy that it installs for each new user. A check of only the signed-in account can miss older copies.

Vitko's test write-up gives two commands to run in a PowerShell window opened as administrator. The first lists every user's copy of Paint, and the second lists the provisioned copy.

Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers -Name Microsoft.Paint | Select-Object Version, @{ n = 'Users'; e = { $_.PackageUserInformation.UserSecurityId.Username -join ', ' } }

Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online | Where-Object DisplayName -eq 'Microsoft.Paint' | Select-Object Version

For any copy below 11.2609.401.0:

  • Update Paint through the Store, or let the Store auto-update install the fixed build. In Intune and other device-management tools, the Store app update scan does this across many PCs.
  • Run both commands again and check that every copy shows 11.2609.401.0 or later.

The advisory lists no workaround or mitigation. Before the fix reached the Store, Vitko suggested removing Paint where nobody needs it, for every user and from the provisioned copy. He did not test that step.

Attack Conditions and Exploitation Status

An attacker could exploit the flaw by sending "a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network," the advisory says, but it does not name the service. The attack would require no sign-in and no user assistance.

The flaw was not in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog run by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency when The Hacker News checked today. The catalog was last updated earlier this week.

articles.title: Malicious Browser Extensions Could Use Claude Dispatch to Run Code on Users' Computers
articles.content:
A browser extension that can run scripts on claude.ai could make Claude Desktop run code on a person's computer, researchers at Forever Security, an endpoint security company, showed in a test.

The attack needs Dispatch, a Claude feature that lets people send tasks from their phone to Claude Desktop. The flaw that makes this possible can still be exploited, the researchers said earlier this week.

Claude Desktop is an AI agent that can run commands on the computer where it is installed. The researchers found that Dispatch also accepted an ordinary signed-in session on claude.ai, the Claude website, even though the site showed no link to it. That let an extension running on the site send Claude Desktop instructions as if the user had sent them.

The researchers say Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, told them on October 13 that Dispatch would be retired, with the end of October as the target. The Dispatch help page, last updated late last week, does not mention a retirement.

It says Dispatch is closed to new users and that people who already use it on some Pro, Max, and Ultra plans "can keep using it for now."

How the Attack Worked

The attack needs two things, according to a technical write-up by Forever Security researcher Gal Weizman: an extension that can run scripts on claude.ai, and a person signed in to both claude.ai and Claude Desktop with Dispatch turned on.

The extension could be malicious, a legitimate one that received a compromised update, or a legitimate one with a security flaw. Dispatch itself only works while the computer is awake and the desktop app is open.

In the test, a script on the user's claude.ai page opened Dispatch and sent Claude four prompts as if it were the user. The prompts asked Claude to install an npm package.

Claude first hesitated over the unfamiliar package, but a follow-up message, delivered in the user's voice, got it to go ahead.

Claude asks before it acts, but those approval prompts appeared in the web page the extension controlled. The script clicked any "Allow" button every second, so no one had to be watching.

Claude then ran a global npm install, and the package's install script opened the Calculator app. No browser exploit was needed. The same step could have stolen files or installed a backdoor, given Claude's permissions on the computer, the researchers say.

The test was run with the browser and Claude Desktop on the same computer, and the researchers report no real attacks. Because Dispatch connects devices, the extension could also reach Claude Desktop on a different computer signed in to the same Claude account, they say. That case is described but not shown.

The same reach could link a home computer to a work laptop when someone uses a single personal Claude account on both devices, with Dispatch turned on. The researchers have seen personal Claude accounts with cross-device Dispatch turned on, on work computers at their customers.

The researchers reported the flaw to Anthropic on May 14. The company accepted it as valid on May 19 but closed the report as a duplicate of an issue it had already found internally, according to the researchers.

"Anthropic is retiring Dispatch, but not the design behind it," the researchers wrote, adding that two other Claude features, Claude Code Remote Control and Claude Cowork sessions, let extensions carry out the same attack. Their write-up does not include a test of those features, and they plan a follow-up post.

What Dispatch Users Can Do

In Claude Desktop, Dispatch is part of Cowork and appears in the left-side panel. The Dispatch help page says users should know how to quickly disconnect or revoke access before turning the feature on, but it does not explain how.

The researchers recommend these steps:

  • Turn off cross-device Dispatch if you do not need it. If you do need it, review how devices are paired, approved, and removed.
  • Treat browser extensions like other software on the computer: check their permissions, control what gets installed, and review updates that give them more access.
  • Monitor what AI agents do on the computer, including unexpected package installations, setting changes, access to credentials, and external connections.

articles.title: Attacks on supermarket and blood storage systems prompt US warning
articles.content:
Attackers don’t have to steal information to cause serious harm. Sometimes, changing a temperature setting is enough.

On November 5, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and three other federal agencies issued a warning urging operators to secure industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems.

The warning follows cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe. Separately, France’s national blood service confirmed that the monitoring and control systems at three of its cold-storage sites had been affected. Staff intervened before any blood products or samples were compromised. The incident showed how a connected cooling system can put essential supplies at risk.

On October 13, after the first attacks in France, refrigeration supplier Danfoss advised its Dutch customers to disconnect their systems from the public internet and reconnect only through a secure network.

A Danfoss spokesperson told NOS that most stores followed the advice. When similar attacks reached the Netherlands on November 2, major supermarket chains were reportedly unaffected. At least 17 businesses, mainly butcher shops and small neighborhood stores, had their refrigeration systems compromised.

Danfoss said that the affected systems were still accessible through unsecured connections and used default passwords. The spokesperson said the attacks could have been prevented if the recommended precautions had been taken.

CISA and its partners warned that attackers may exploit authentication bypass flaws, code-injection vulnerabilities, or weak configurations in refrigeration controllers. Successful attacks could let them change temperatures or force equipment into continuous heating or defrost cycles.

The agencies recommend reducing that risk by keeping control panels off the public internet, isolating operational equipment from business networks, changing default passwords, using strong authentication, patching firmware, and replacing unsupported devices. They also recommend setting safe operating limits and alerts for temperature changes outside those limits.

What about home appliances?

You don’t need an industrial refrigeration unit to adopt some of these precautions.

  • Check whether you need remote access. If you never use a device while away from home, disable that feature. Check the manufacturer’s instructions first; disabling remote access may also affect alerts or smart-home integrations.
  • Check who can access the appliance, including suppliers, and how that access is protected.
  • Change default passwords and secure the associated account. Use a strong password and enable two-step verification wherever the appliance or app supports it. Protecting the app account matters as well as protecting the appliance itself.
  • Keep firmware and apps updated. Turn on automatic updates where available, and don’t ignore manual update prompts.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.”

articles.title: Railway’s AI agents go off the track on a rival’s network
articles.content:
Railway says an engineer’s AI testing tool went too far while probing cloud rival Primcloud, stressing that he acted independently of the company.

AI agents operated by cloud infrastructure and application hosting platform, Railway, have attempted to access a rival platform’s infrastructure, prompting the cloud provider’s leadership to acknowledge the incident on social media.

Railway senior product engineer Jake Runzer acknowledged running agents to perform signups and agentic testing on similar platforms after Primcloud founder Josh Manders publicly questioned why Railway employees were attempting to breach his infrastructure.

Runzer said he had halted the testing harness after it began reaching too far. Railway co-founder and CEO Jake Cooper apologized, saying the models were “getting a bit too good at this point,” and pledged to prohibit non-manual external testing.

According to Manders, the agents attempted to receive credentials from an application container, request platform secrets, access cloud-provider metadata, discover internal databases and caches, and scan all 65,536 addresses on Primcloud’s internal network twice.

The activity reportedly involved 24 scripted commands over 15 minutes.

“An agent can act without a person directing every step,” said Diana Kelley, chief information security officer at Noma Security. “It doesn’t remove the responsibility of the people and organizations that deploy it.”

Primcloud said its defenses blocked every attempt and that “nothing” was accessed. The incident follows Railway’s own security disclosure involving encrypted customer environment variables.

The engineer was acting on his own

Cooper said the employee had developed the testing tool independently, using personal accounts, a personal credit card, and his own time. He added that Runzer ran it against a single external provider and halted it proactively within 15 minutes, adding that Railway had addressed the incident internally.

“I can confirm they ran this tool once and only once,” Cooper said in an X post. “Railway does not condone these actions. We expect all our employees to uphold our standards of conduct, whether acting on behalf of Railway or in a personal capacity.”

Although that timeline checks out with Manders’ own account, some details remain murky. After publicly calling out Runzer on X, Manders posted a follow-up, saying he had observed another attempt to access the account after his initial warning.

“I see you tried to access the account after this tweet too, Jake,” he had written more than 30 minutes after his first post.

Primcloud does not have a bug bounty program, according to its Acceptable Use Policy (AUP). It forbids unauthorized probing, scanning, or vulnerability testing without prior written consent.

‘The AI did it’ is not an accountability strategy

Experts condemn Railway’s “rogue AI” explanation for the incident.

Amir Boldo, co-founder and chief product and technology officer of Above Security, cautioned against describing agents as attackers, as they can execute attacker-like sequences without any malicious intent.

Execution traces can establish what an agent did, but they cannot independently prove intent, he said, adding that investigators need evidence spanning instructions, identities, permissions, inputs and tool calls. “You can’t put an agent on trial. You can hold each party accountable for its part,” Boldo said.

Ronald Lewis, head of cybersecurity governance at Black Duck, argued that users may not fully appreciate that delegating work to an agent also delegates the authority associated with their identity.

“We now have to ask what happens when trusted identity is delegated to a non-deterministic system capable of independently deciding how to use it,” Lewis said. Cooper confirmed in his X post that Railway had addressed the incident internally and was reinforcing its expectations for employee conduct, including when employees act in a personal capacity.

articles.title: CPython flaw exposes AI inference servers to sandbox escape attacks
articles.content:
RunSybil demonstrated code execution through a malicious model template. Python says the sandbox escapes fall outside its security threat model.

A memory-safety flaw in CPython can allow malicious AI model templates to escape code sandboxes and execute arbitrary code inside inference servers, according to security researchers at RunSybil.

“By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests,” Darius Houle, a security researcher at RunSybil, wrote in a blog post. “They also could strike directly at the underlying cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads.”

The researchers demonstrated how a specially crafted model could exploit the flaw to bypass Jinja, a Python-based templating engine used to structure interactions between users and LLMs, sandbox protections, and execute code in the process of serving the model. The attack could expose AI hosting providers that allow customers to upload and run their own models, potentially giving attackers a foothold inside infrastructure processing requests for multiple customers, the post added.

However, the Python Security Response Team (PSRT), which handles security reports involving CPython, disputed the security implications of the demonstration in a response to CSO. “We acknowledge the underlying CPython bug reported by RunSybil and appreciate their contribution to fixing it. However, we do not consider the demonstrated sandbox escape to be a CPython security vulnerability,” the team said.

The disagreement centres on whether the interpreter should be responsible for preventing sandbox escapes. While RunSybil argues that the flaw creates risks for AI inference infrastructure, PSRT says executing untrusted Python code within a sandbox is outside CPython’s security threat model.

Exploiting Python’s type-handling mechanism

“The bug we discovered abuses CPython’s handling of generic types to accomplish a breakout,” Houle wrote. “We exploited it using objects that sandboxes make available in every template, even in empty sandbox contexts.”

The researchers found that CPython can use a cached list of parameters even after an object has been modified through a callback. When the interpreter subsequently looks for a newly introduced parameter in the original list, it can receive an invalid index. An assertion designed to catch the condition is disabled in normal release builds, allowing the interpreter to access memory outside the expected bounds.

RunSybil used this behavior to retrieve references to Python objects that the sandbox was supposed to keep inaccessible.

“While an invalid address will generally crash the interpreter, an address pointing to a useful live Python object gives our callback a reference to that object (even when the sandbox never intends to expose it),” Houle wrote.

The researchers then used the recovered object references to access Python classes and functions needed to construct executable code.

Malicious model templates enable code execution

To demonstrate the attack, RunSybil modified the Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct model by inserting a backdoored chat_template.jinja file. When the model was loaded and used through an inference-serving engine such as vLLM, the template enabled arbitrary code execution in the serving process.

“Breaking out of the chat template sandbox and executing code represents a supply chain risk that endangers inference providers, library developers, and model users,” Houle wrote.

The researchers said they shared proof-of-concept exploits with multiple inference providers supporting bring-your-own-model (BYOM) features, which allow customers to upload models from external sources.

Python disputes vulnerability classification

RunSybil disclosed the issue to CPython, the Pallets Project, which maintains Jinja, and Hugging Face. The researchers said they encountered conflicting views about which project should address the underlying problem.

CPython maintains that the interpreter does not support sandboxing untrusted Python code as a security boundary. In its response to CSO, the PSRT referred to the project’s security policy, which states that sandbox escapes should be addressed by the maintainers of the affected sandboxing software.

“Escapes from such sandboxes are therefore outside our security threat model and should be addressed by the maintainers of the affected sandboxing software,” the team said.

The team also disputed RunSybil’s suggestion that there was no coordinated remediation process. It said the researchers had submitted the report by email rather than through CPython’s designated private GitHub vulnerability reporting channel.

Fix backported to three Python branches

RunSybil submitted a patch to CPython, which was merged into the main development branch on Aug. 14. According to the PSRT, the fix was also backported to the 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 branches as a regular bug fix rather than a security fix.

The distinction matters because RunSybil had raised concerns that the fix would not reach all supported Python versions.

The researchers said the absence of a backport to Python 3.12 could delay adoption of the fix across AI infrastructure deployments.

“With major portions of the AI ecosystem still solidly aligned on Python 3.12, we might not see organic adoption of our memory-safety fixes until late 2028, when it reaches its end-of-life date,” Houle wrote. The researchers recommend that AI hosting providers treat sandboxed code, template engines and expression evaluators as best-effort security controls rather than relying on them as standalone security boundaries.

articles.title: A 10-minute Spinal Stretching Routine to Alleviate Lower Back Pain
articles.content:
After a long stretch of sitting, even standing up or turning to look behind you can feel uncomfortable. When your back feels stiff and in pain, the goal is not to force a deeper stretch. It is to find movements you can perform comfortably and build from there.

Gentle, yoga-inspired exercises can help you explore bending, extending, and rotating your back with greater control. Alongside appropriate strengthening and regular physical activity, they may help ease discomfort and make everyday movement easier.

Exercises to Relieve Spinal Discomfort

You can try this set of exercises designed to mobilize the spine. However, if you are experiencing significant pain or have conditions such as a herniated disc or sciatica, you should first consult a medical professional or physical therapist for an assessment before trying the exercises. Also, never force your body to reach the maximum range of motion.

1. Open Book

Step 1: Lie on your side with knees bent at 90 degrees and arms extended straight out in front of you.

Step 2: Open your top arm toward the opposite side until it is close to the floor, rotating your upper back; follow your hand with your gaze.

Step 3: Repeat on the other side.

2. Side-Lying Rotation

Step 1: Lie face down with arms extended at your sides.

Step 2: Bend one arm to support your body while bending the leg on the same side behind you, rotating your torso.

Step 3: Repeat on the other side.

3. Mermaid Stretch

Step 1: Lie face down with hands placed at your sides, arms bent, and palms pressing against the floor.

Step 2: Exhale as you slowly push your upper body up with your hands, looking up.

Step 3: Inhale while slowly returning to the face-down position.

4. Child’s Pose to Puppy Pose

Step 1: Kneel on the floor with hands supporting you; sit back toward your heels, then bring your head close to the floor, and slowly extend your arms forward to relax your back.

Step 2: Slowly shift your body weight forward, lowering your forearms to the floor while lifting your hips.

5. Shoulder Stretch

Step 1: Kneel on the floor with your toes tucked under; slowly extend your arms forward, lower your forearms to the floor, and lift your hips.

Step 2: Slowly lower your chest toward the floor, bringing it as close as possible to feel the stretch in your shoulders, chest, and back.

6. Seated Side Bend

Step 1: Sit upright with a straight back.

Step 2: Raise your right arm high, then bend and stretch it toward the left side.

Step 3: Return to the starting position, then raise your left arm high and bend and stretch it toward the right side.

7. Lifting and Sinking

Step 1: Sit with your back straight.

Step 2: As you exhale, slowly tilt your pelvis backward, allowing your spine to curve and your head to lower gradually.

Step 3: As you inhale, slowly lift your pelvis upward, extending and straightening your spine vertebra by vertebra, while lifting your head and looking straight ahead.

8. Round Back–Hinge Forward

Step 1: Sit upright with your back straight, legs loosely crossed and hands resting on your knees.

Step 2: As you exhale, tilt your pelvis backward to curve your spine and shift your center of gravity slightly rearward; hold onto your knees with your hands to maintain balance.

Step 3: As you inhale, slowly lift your pelvis upward, extending and straightening your spine vertebra by vertebra, while leaning your upper body forward as close to your knees as possible.

9. Seated Spinal Twist

Step 1: Sit with your back straight.

Step 2: Slowly rotate your body to the right, placing your left hand on your right knee.

Step 3: Return to the starting position, then slowly rotate your body to the left, placing your right hand on your left knee. Avoid rapid or forceful twisting of the waist.

10. Knee Hug Stretch

Step 1: Sit with your knees bent, holding your lower legs with your hands and keeping your chest close to your knees.

Step 2: Slowly shift your center of gravity backward, lowering your back onto the floor while using your hands to pull your knees toward your chest.

Step 3: Slowly move your knees away from your body, then use your hands to pull them back toward your chest. Repeat the movement.

Let Comfort Guide Your Progress

Start with just a few slow repetitions of the movements that feel comfortable. For a held stretch, pause for a few easy breaths rather than pushing farther. Gradually add repetitions or time as the movements become easier, and reduce the range or skip an exercise if symptoms increase.

A useful routine is one you can return to comfortably. Pair these mobility exercises with regular walking or other activity you enjoy, and build strength gradually with guidance when needed.

articles.title: OpenSSH flaw lets attackers access password-disabled accounts on some Linux systems
articles.content:
The trivial exploit involves sending an arbitrary extra-long password to an OpenSSH server running on a vulnerable Linux configuration, including the popular Alpine Linux.

A critical vulnerability that affects OpenSSH servers on Linux systems built with the musl C library instead of glibc allows remote attackers to easily bypass authentication and log into accounts that should have password authentication disabled. The flaw impacts the lightweight Alpine Linux, which is widely used for cloud Docker container images, as well as Linux distributions for embedded systems.

The security bug, dubbed *SSHole and tracked as CVE-2026-123158, was discovered by Ozgun Kultekin, a researcher with security testing firm Wakefield, and has existed for the past 10 years. The OpenSSH maintainers moved quickly to add mitigation for the flaw in the OpenSSH 10.6p2 emergency update released Thursday, even though they claim the bug is not actually in their code.

“It’s not every day that the ‘exploit’ for a vulnerability in a technology as prevalent as OpenSSH is just ‘send a long password’ or ‘send a lot of A characters,’ but here we are,” said Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at preemptive exposure management firm watchTowr. “On affected systems, the exploit is strikingly simple: send a password between 257 and 1,024 characters long.”

Luckily, there are some prerequisites for this exploit to work:

  • The Linux distribution needs to use musl, which means that many popular server distros such as Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora are not impacted
  • The system needs to use OpenSSH and not alternative SSH server implementations such as Dropbear, which many embedded distros use
  • OpenSSH needs to be configured without support for Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), the most common Linux login framework
  • OpenSSH needs to allow password-based authentication
  • The attacker needs to know the name of an account for which password login has been disabled at the system level

Those conditions are met in default configuration for Alpine Linux and its built-in “alpine” username, which allows executing commands as root. The Alpine project released emergency updates for the openssh package and advises users who can’t update to disable password-based authentication in the OpenSSH configuration and set up key-based authentication.

Why the trivial attack works

The flaw is the product of three changes made years apart, each solving a different problem. In 2012, musl’s developers capped password length at 256 bytes to stop attackers from tying up server resources by sending long passwords that need to be hashed as part of the login verification process.

At the same time they also made the library’s password hashing function return an asterisk (*) whenever it fails. The asterisk is the same character Unix has used since the 1980s to mark accounts for which no password should ever match — accounts with password disabled at the system level.

In 2016, OpenSSH changed how it checks passwords for accounts whose own password field offers no salt to hash against, borrowing another account’s salt so that attackers could not guess existing usernames with brute-force login retries and timing the server’s responses. Then in 2022, Alpine switched root’s password field to an asterisk so that SSH key logins would keep working for it.

When an attacker sends an over-long password for a password-disabled account on such a system, the hash attempt fails and returns an asterisk, which sshd compares with the asterisk stored in the account’s password field. The two match, and the login succeeds.

Alpine Linux cloud images will be the main target

Alpine’s standard OpenSSH package is built without PAM, and password logins are enabled by default, so Alpine servers meet the conditions out of the box. On the official cloud images published between versions 3.18.11 and 3.24.3, the default user account, named alpine, is one of the password-disabled accounts, and the images grant it passwordless “doas” privileges.

As a result, an attacker who logs in as that user can then switch to root, so the images are exposed as soon as an administrator sets a password for any other account on the system, because a legitimate account with a real password needs to exist for this attack to work.

Unlike the critical regreSSHion flaw from 2024, this one is confined to the musl world, but it requires no exploit engineering of any kind.

“Internet-exposed SSH servers are already being hammered by password guesses and brute-force attempts around the clock,” Knott said. “Exploiting this vulnerability simply means those same attackers add a very long password attempt to that brute-force list. We’d be extremely surprised if we didn’t see SSH brute-forcers attempting this by the weekend.”

Organizations should also check whether the flaw was already used against their servers. An “Accepted password” entry in /var/log/messages for an account that has no password, such as root, a key-only user, or the default alpine user, is a strong sign of compromise.

Alpine recommends reviewing doas usage, recently created users and files on exposed machines, and its advisory says any server where a login cannot be ruled out should be treated as compromised. Kultekin also published a check script on GitHub that identifies exposed servers and lists the accounts at risk.

articles.title: French banking group hit by supply chain cyberattack
articles.content:
The attack via a third-party provider’s platform gave crooks access to an internal account at Crédit Mutuel Arkéa.

French regional banking group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa admitted Wednesday that attackers had accessed an internal account via an unnamed third-party service provider’s platform and transferred funds to other financial institutions. Those funds, it said, could have then been potentially converted to cryptocurrency by the thieves.

The day before, cryptocurrency news outlet CoinDesk reported that the attack had been detected on Monday by blockchain investigator ZachXBT, although at the time he did not identify the entity involved. On Wednesday, he identified the suspected victim as Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, which the banking group later confirmed. It did not, however, specify whether the stolen funds were originally in traditional currency or cryptocurrency.

This attack comes amidst worries by European regulators about cyber threats to financial institutions as they become more reliant on interconnected systems and external service providers.

The bank, which serves the West of France, temporarily suspended some transactions in the wake of the attack to prevent further fraudulent activity. It reported that, as of Wednesday morning, operations were returning to normal after the implementation of additional security controls. French law enforcement is investigating the breach.

In its initial announcement, the group reassured customers that their funds were safe. “This incident has no impact on [customer] assets, and has only resulted in a delayed execution of certain transfer operations. Their interests are fully protected, and safeguarding their assets is an absolute priority,” it said.

French regional newspaper Le Télégramme reported that the thieves had taken over €118 million (over $133 million); the bank would not confirm the amount but said that the order of magnitude was accurate.

The bank said it was still working to assess the precise financial consequences of this attack. “Some of the funds involved have been frozen, and other actions are underway to recover them. While it is therefore still too early to provide a final figure, we can already confirm that the amounts involved are in no way likely to jeopardize the financial health and stability of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa,” it said. The group has 5.8 million customers and manages more than €211 billion (about $237 billion) in assets.

articles.title: Phone return scams: where a real delivery and a fake return end up in a bill for you
articles.content:
A caller offers you a free phone upgrade or an exclusive deal from your mobile provider. A new phone arrives at your home. So far, everything seems to check out.

Then comes another call: There’s been a shipping mistake. You received the wrong phone, and the company needs you to send it back. You send it back, but the phone never reaches your provider, leaving you with a large charge or long-term contract to pay.

Now police are warning about this scheme after residents lost devices and were left facing the associated payments.

How phone return scams work

The scam usually starts with a call from a spoofed number. In the US we’re seeing several examples in anonymized Malwarebytes Scam Guard records of the impersonated company being Canadian mobile provider Rogers.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre warns:

“After collecting personal information required for credit checks, they’ll order a new phone in your name.”

Next, a genuine device arrives through a legitimate delivery service. That delivery makes the next part of the story easier to believe.

The caller gets back in touch and claims something went wrong. Perhaps the company sent the wrong device, or an extra phone arrived by mistake. To put things right, you need to send it back using the label or shipping QR code they provide.

The shipping label is the real trick. Rather than directing the package to the provider’s returns facility, it sends the device to an address chosen by the criminals.

The result: You no longer have the phone, but your provider has not received it back. Victims can be left facing a contract, financing agreement, or monthly payments for the missing device.

How to stay safe

The most important protection against most types of scams is having someone you can trust and help you decide whether something is a scam. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can be that partner if you’re on your own.

You don’t need to decide on the spot about whether a caller sounds convincing. Break the conversation and verify the offer separately. Pause and check if you encounter any of the following:

  • An unexpected call offering a free phone, loyalty reward, or unusually attractive upgrade.
  • A caller asking for personal, financial, or account information to arrange the offer.
  • A follow-up call claiming the wrong device was shipped or that another delivery mistake needs correcting.
  • Instructions to use a return label or QR code supplied by that caller.
  • A return destination that you have not confirmed directly with your provider.

If you’ve already sent a phone, contact your mobile provider immediately using verified contact details. Explain that you believe you were targeted by a phone return scam, identify the affected orders, and ask for a fraud investigation.

If you shared your account password or PIN, change it through the provider’s official channels. Rogers advises customers who disclosed their credentials to reset them and contact customer service to check for unauthorized transactions.

Keep the evidence: messages, emails, the shipping label, tracking details, order confirmations, bills, and a timeline of the calls. These records can help support a billing complaint and fraud report.

articles.title: NIKKE PC launcher compromise put players’ passwords and personal files at risk
articles.content:
Players of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE are being urged to check their PCs after attackers tampered with files used by the game’s Windows launcher. Opening the launcher could allow malicious software to run, potentially exposing much more than a player’s game account.

The incident occurred as part of a supply-chain attack, where services or software used by the company in question is compromised. In practice, this meant that instead of persuading players to download a fake game or install a suspicious add-on, the attackers compromised resources used by the legitimate launcher. Players could therefore encounter the threat simply by opening software they already trusted.

Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client. However, fixing the delivery mechanism does not undo an infection, nor does it recover passwords and other information that may have been stolen.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

Independent researcher MotherSphere identified malicious code in four JavaScript files hosted on Level Infinite’s official content delivery network (CDN).

Players should be aware of a discrepancy in the published timelines. Level Infinite says malicious-program distribution began on October 30, while MotherSphere reports evidence of the remote-control agent running as early as October 23.

According to the researcher’s analysis, the distributed remote-control agent supported commands to:

  • Run programs and system commands.
  • Browse folders and download files.
  • Take screenshots.
  • Retrieve saved NIKKE login credentials.
  • Collect browser passwords and cookies.
  • Search for developer credentials, API tokens, and other secrets.
  • Collect cryptocurrency wallet-extension data.

The number of compromised PCs and the full extent of any data theft remain unclear.

How to stay safe

Mobile-only players are not affected, according to Level Infinite, so they do not need to take any additional security measures.

Level Infinite says it replaced three abnormal script files early on November 4, then refreshed the CDN’s cache for the remaining file later that day. MotherSphere subsequently reported that all four files were clean on the four CDN servers checked.

If you opened the Windows launcher during the period identified above, take the following steps.

  • Close the launcher and check your PC. MotherSphere’s report includes user-reported Malwarebytes detections for traces associated with the attack.
  • Follow the removal instructions published by NIKKE carefully.
  • Secure your accounts from a clean device. Do not change passwords on a computer that may still be compromised.
  • If a cryptocurrency wallet or its recovery phrase may have been exposed, use a clean device to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new recovery phrase.
  • Level Infinite asks players who believe they were affected, including those experiencing problems with external accounts or financial losses, to contact its customer support team, so keep relevant records without handing over personal information.

Please note that the NIKKE wiki’s unofficial cleanup guidance recommends scanning with Malwarebytes. Although the guide describes this as a one-time free option, Malwarebytes Free lets you continue running manual scans and removing detected malware after the Premium trial ends. The trial provides additional features, including real-time protection, so decide what is best for you.

From reporting threats to removing them.

A signature buried in pages of electronic paperwork should never substitute for that understanding. Anyone who has checked into a medical office knows the drill. Read this. Sign here. Accept that. Vaccination should require a separate, clearly documented authorization. Explain the proposed treatment, its risks, and its expected benefits. Give parents time to ask questions. articles.title: Scammers use AI-generated images of missing pets to extort owners
articles.content:
When your pet goes missing, it can be totally heartbreaking.

So hearing that they’ve been found is no doubt very welcome news. Even better to see a photo of them looking safe and well.

But while the photo may look exactly like your pet, that doesn’t mean the person who sent it has your pet or even ever saw it.

The BBC reports how criminals are sending owners AI-generated images of their missing pets, demanding money for their return, and sometimes threatening to harm the animals when owners refuse to pay.

The BBC interviewed two targets of this scam who were both contacted after posting a missing pet message on social media. The scammers sent them pictures of their beloved pets and demanded a ransom for their safe return.

Messages like these exploit two powerful emotions in quick succession: relief that a beloved pet has been found, followed by fear that something terrible will happen unless the owner acts immediately.

The scam typically follows this pattern:

  • A scammer finds a missing pet appeal, which is typically posted to social media or local sites with an accompanying photo and contact details.
  • The scammer contacts the owner and claims to have found the animal. An image fabricated with the help of AI makes the claim appear more convincing.
  • They ask for money which may be described as a reward or as payment for emergency treatment.
  • They add pressure. They might refuse to meet until payment arrives, or threaten to sell or harm the pet.

Our data backs this report up. Over the last month, people anonymously submitted three distinctive types of pet related scam attempts to Malwarebytes Scam Guard:

  • “We found your missing cat” message, with photos: Someone claimed to have found a user’s missing cat and had images of it.
  • Found pet callback lure: A voicemail claimed to have found a lost cat and supplied a callback number.
  • Humane Society impersonation and payment demand: A caller claimed a missing cat needed emergency surgery, and demanded successive Zelle payments.

How to stay safe

Sadly, while it can be very useful to use social media to retrieve lost pets, it also attracts scammers and other abuse.

You don’t have to stop asking for help online, but you can put some safeguards between an unexpected message and any payment.

  • Keep some identifying details private. Leave a distinctive feature out of the public description so you can ask a supposed finder about it later.
  • Do not pay in advance to secure a reunion. Be particularly wary of someone who insists that you send money before they will let you see the animal. Arrange any legitimate handover in a safe, public location, and verify that it is your pet before paying a reward.
  • Verify veterinary claims independently. If someone says your pet is at an animal hospital, find the hospital’s contact details yourself and call it directly. Do not rely on the number or payment link in the message.
  • A second pair of eyes can help you assess a demand without the same emotional pressure. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can help you identify whether a message might be a scam and how to proceed.
  • If someone is threatening your pet, remember that when they make threats to your pet, it is very likely they don’t have a clue where it is either, so don’t let them extort you.

articles.title: Formaldehyde found after Toledo chemical leak
articles.content:
Podcast: Play in new window | Download | Embed

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | iHeartRadio | Podcast Index | RSS

A family should not need a lawyer on retainer or a chemistry degree to find out whether home is safe after a chemical leak. Yet that is the burden communities face when ordinary residents suddenly find themselves up against powerful industries.

The chemical release in Toledo has raised questions that reach beyond one neighborhood. Elizabeth Frost, co-founder of Independent Force and an advocate working with affected residents, sees troubling similarities to the response after the East Palestine train derailment.

Her concern is straightforward: When industry helps shape the response and selects testing contractors, residents have reason to question whose interests come first.

Frost describes families struggling to understand possible exposures while receiving reassurances that do not resolve their concerns. She points to independent testing and cautions about burning potentially contaminated leaves as examples of information residents need while questions remain unanswered.

The chemicals and circumstances differ between Toledo and East Palestine. The imbalance facing residents feels painfully familiar.

People dealing with unexpected medical bills, frightening symptoms, and uncertainty about their homes should not have to carry the burden of proving what happened alone. East Palestine residents have told Frost they want their suffering to mean something. They want the next community treated differently.

That hope also belongs in the voting booth.

Americans frustrated with both major parties have opportunities closer to home than a presidential campaign. Independent candidates face enormous financial and ballot-access hurdles nationally. County commissions, state legislative districts, and congressional races offer more manageable paths.

Local leadership matters. Communities can organize help, confront controversial development proposals, and elect people willing to pursue practical solutions.

The work ahead is to make room for independent ideas and candidates, including people willing to work across party lines. Encourage capable neighbors to run. Participate locally. A healthier country needs citizens who refuse to remain spectators.

Hello everyone and welcome to another edition of The Lowdown. I’m Jeff Louderback and we’re into November now. Obviously, when you’re listening to this, it’ll be it a day or more after, but we’re recording this on election day, and it’s been a it’s been pretty fascinating leading up to election day. It it’s different for me because for four and a half years I’ve had been a national reporter at the Epic Times and then covering elections and high-profile races, and as listeners know on here about a two months ago I stepped out back out on my own to focus on articles and book projects and and to have more freedom and flexibility.

But what I’m doing is covering Maha elections now, meaning pro-Maha candidates, and they have them all across the country, and and we’ll get into that a little bit more later in the show. I’d like to introduce my guest. She’s been on before, Elizabeth Frost, who’s the co-founder of Independent Force and is she’s with Maha Ohio. And welcome to the show, Elizabeth.

Yeah, thank you so much for having me, Jeff. I’m glad to be here. And it’s interesting. I know we have a lot of things to talk about, and maybe let’s start with.

I know you had reached out to me about something that I didn’t even know about because I’ve been so focused on other projects, but someone mentioned in passing that there was a chemical leak up in northwest Ohio in the Toledo area, but I hadn’t really researched it until you brought it to my attention because you you wanted to share something about the chemical leak and also the the urging to not burn leaves and branches. Let’s dive into that if you could tell our listeners, give them the 101 on that subject. Absolutely. So I’ll start from the top on the evening of Tuesday, October 20th.

So at this point, we’re coming up on two weeks. And depending on when listeners are actually hearing this, it times could vary and timelines could vary. So I do want to make just a a quick note that this advice or any guidance that we’re giving is is very fluid before we get into this, because depending on when viewers are listening to this, the best way for them to handle the exposure situation could change. But on the evening of October 20th, just about two weeks ago, there was a tank facility called MC Tank in Toledo, which is is right in this industrial area of Toledo, near a Jeep factory.

And, there’s a lot of residential housing and apartment buildings that are within, a half a mile and one mile radius of where this occurred as well. And the chemical that leaked is something called glycidyl methacrylate, which is easiest for conversation purposes. We’ll call it GMA. And GMA is an industrial chemical that’s used as a surface coating.

It’s not a PFAS, which I’ve been getting that question a lot, but it is a pretty nasty chemical. In America and honestly, just the world, we’re really lacking a lot of information that I think we’d like to have as far as what happens when a human is exposed to something like GMA, or what breakdown products does GMA turn into when it’s in different weather conditions like fog or sunlight. And we just don’t know all of the answers to those questions because there are so many different chemistries in the world. Industry is always coming up with new things, and the research system, as broken as it is, even when folks are really trying, just cannot keep up with everything that we need to know.

So unfortunately, the situation in Toledo has left us with a lot of questions, and I don’t want to call the residents who are affected by this guinea pigs by any means, but we unfortunately just are not gonna know certain things until we start to see how folks are reacting to this to this chemical spill. But, to paint the picture of what that night would have been like for a resident in Toledo, we’ve heard a lot of stories and a lot of testimonies from folks who have recounted what happened. And when this chemical leak occurred, it created a massive plume, and and people can find pictures of that online. And that massive plume ended up getting caught in some low-level fog that was already on the ground in Toledo or starting to build on the ground in Toledo.

And ideally, if something like this were to happen, you would want those chemicals to go straight up as far away from humans as possible, dissipate, and then any exposure situations that would happen would be much less concentrated. But unfortunately, in this case, that wasn’t able to happen because of the fog and a cold pocket of weather that was sitting above Toledo that night. So ultimately, as far as we can tell, what happened is that these chemicals were trapped in that fog and essentially rolled down the terrain in Toledo and surrounding areas, ultimately coding these residential neighborhoods in this fog. So folks were trying to leave after they were noticing there was a weird smell and things didn’t look right outside.

Sometime in the middle of the night, an evacuation order came in for folks that were within a one mile radius. And so people are starting to hear about this. In some cases, several hours after the leak occurred. If you hadn’t been looking outside, people just didn’t know what was going on.

And by the time people are trying to leave, the fog is is so dense, people are reporting they couldn’t see a foot in front of them. There’s these weird white particles in the fog, which appears to have been the GMA reacting with the water vapor. And so people were were trying to leave in this really chaotic, almost apocalyptic type situation. And so that leaves us with where we are now, that we’re we’re trying to gather as much good advice and good evidence as we can for the residents of Toledo and get this information out to them because there are just a lot of unanswered questions.

We are starting to figure out through testing that’s being done by Blue Shirt Justice Group that there is formaldehyde on the ground in Toledo. And there has been in the days and weeks since this derominant occurred, and that is a byproduct of GMA. And so, now our concern is is shifting to what are these byproducts in addition to trying to understand what could come downstream for these residents from that initial exposure. Yeah, this sounds very familiar.

And I know we’re gonna talk about an update on East Palestine here in a few minutes, but what what is the community doing about are the municipalities and as a state responded? And what can you tell us about that? Sure. So, as in in pretty much any chemical spill or disaster response situation, we have been seeing the health department sending out communications to residents, advising them, of washing their hands and going to the ER if anything is concerning them, if they’re they’re noticing any type of respiratory issues.

But then we’re also seeing the mayor of Toledo making comments, urging people that it’s okay to come home. There was on day one, it really took me back. There is this interview that the mayor of Toledo had done where he said something to the effect of yes, my nose and my eyes and my throat are burning too, but that doesn’t mean that this is anything serious. It’s just surface level irritation.

And so you had the resident or the the mayor of Toledo telling residents to ignore it, essentially, if their nose or their eyes were burning and that it was just an irritant. But we do have some data that in the United States, GMA is considered carcinogenic in animals. And in the EU, GMA is considered probably carcinogenic to humans. So we do have some in vitro research, just meaning, human tissue outside of the body research that has been done that does show that this is both genotoxic to humans, meaning it can damage your DNA.

But it’s also downstream of that likely to be highly carcinogenic. Again, we’re just lacking a lot of this, all lacking a lot of the research that we would need to be able to make definitive statements about this, but all signs do point toward this being carcinogenic in humans, including animal testing. And so that the that type of response coming from a public official is very concerning. I know that memos that we’ve sent out about not burning leaves because the GMA and byproducts, have likely coated those leaves.

And it, combustion just creates more unpredictable chemicals in addition to making you more vulnerable to being exposed to those chemicals when they’re in the air now inside your home or in your yard on your property. We all know when you’re burning anything outside, you smell it. And if you smell it, that means that those particles, at least to some small extent, are making their way over to you and into your airways. And so very important that residents are hearing this type of information.

We have been sending that out to local officials in Toledo. What we’re seeing is is a much more cookie-cutter response as far as the local officials go. Health department is telling people to go to the hospital, but not really being overly direct with any warnings about how dangerous this could be. And then we have the local mayor, who is is wanting to bring everyone home.

And I will add, that I’m sure the mayor is under quite a bit of pressure from the car manufacturing industry and other businesses in Toledo, to get people home and to move things forward. And so it’s a really complicated position for any mayor to be in, but that’s what we’re seeing nonetheless. And looking up at the state level, this is also very par for the course. Ohio seems to be monitoring the situation, but mostly passing the buck up to EPA.

We did see EPA on the ground in Toledo within, I believe, about 24 hours, maybe within 48 hours of this occurring. And that is something that we usually see is that the EPA buses and vans, et cetera, will pull up. But once again, something that’s not incredibly surprising, we have seen this before, is that it does appear that EPA is going to allow industry to handpick a contractor to do a lot of this testing. There is, I believe, some direct EPA testing that’s going on right now, with some controversy that the equipment that they’re using may not be able to detect the types of chemicals that we’re really should be concerned about right now.

But then, we we also have this concern that industry is paying contractors to do a lot of the work that people assume that, hey, this is what my taxes are for, right? We pay a lot of taxes. And, if we’re sending however much to the EPA, I think most people would like to think, that the EPA would be able to do some testing themselves rather than putting this in the hands of industry where they’re able to pick contractors that can can help them with with the results and the way that things all come out at the end of the day. So, if we have time, I think that that contractor piece of this conversation is is really important and relevant to East Palestine as well.

But, regardless, I would encourage the listeners, anytime there’s a chemical response situation, be very mindful of who did the testing and who it is that’s telling you that everything’s fine. Yeah, and this is very eerily similar to a lot that I that I discovered when I was covering the East Palestine aftermath. That’s it’s it’s pretty astonishing, actually, that and I know the testing, what what type of third-party testing is being done? Is that has it gotten to that point yet?

Thankfully, an independent research group called Blue Shirt Justice League, and they were on the ground in Toledo within about 24 to 36 hours after this leak happened, and they brought some pretty fancy equipment that’s a little bit over my head in terms of how it all works. But essentially, it creates a fingerprint. So you don’t exactly have to know what you’re looking for when you go into this is an air, an air testing machine. And so you don’t necessarily have to know what you’re looking for.

Obviously, it helps to have an idea, but it essentially creates a fingerprint for that chemical that you can then take back and figure out okay, what is this thing? And so they brought that into Toledo to do air testing. They also did swipe sampling, which takes much longer to get the results back, unfortunately, but very important to figure out what chemicals may have settled on surfaces and inside and outside of people’s homes. It’s a very, very important piece of information for us to figure out because just because outside the GMA is starting to turn into formaldehyde, GMA can survive a lot longer inside people’s homes when it’s not exposed to sunlight.

And we’re also not completely sure that it’s not going to turn into, other unexpected chemicals that we’re not really looking at or watching for right now. But I will say one good piece of good news from Blue Shirt Justice Group’s testing that they did airwise in Toledo on ground zero the day after the derailment is that they found no GMA lingering in the air. So that was, a piece of positive news because what that tells us is that, the residents that were outside breathing weren’t necessarily breathing the GMA anymore, or at least, at detectable levels at that time. But unfortunately what they did find was formaldehyde.

And that confirmed a lot of theories and suspicions that the combination of that moisture from the fog and the sunlight had started creating this chemical reaction. And formaldehyde, we do have a little bit more information about in terms of human exposure. Which in this line of work is something that you have to consider a silver lining, is that at least we do know a little bit more about formaldehyde, even though we wish people we weren’t having to ask these questions. But I’m very, very, very grateful for Blue Shirt Justice Group and Scott Smith, who is the founder of that group.

They take donations and work with attorneys who help chemical response victims. And they just go out and and do this completely independent of the government, completely independent of industry. So in these situations, there are very everyday people who don’t have an attorney on retainer and have never even thought about those kinds of things. Maybe they don’t have a primary care doctor, and maybe they don’t have a thousand dollars in their bank account. These these residents have an insurmountable challenge to prove, that whatever health issues they might be dealing with, that are costing them, their quality of life, a lot of financial strain, and in many cases other consequences as well, they have to prove that this is actually a causal connection, meaning that this condition that was caused by this chemical that was brought into their lives without their permission. And that is that is a Herculean feat. And that’s that’s what I found when I started working with residents in East Palestine. Yes. And that’s because when your DNA is damaged, you are the the the number of ways that that could go bad for you are says essentially endless, right? That that can cause a number of complications for you health-wise. And so it’s not always as clean cut as, let’s say if you’re exposed to GMA, you’re at an increased risk for non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

It’s it’s much more complex than that. And it’s it’s what we’ve noticed in East Palestine, for example, is that a lot of folks, are in addition to cancers and male breast cancer, for example, is up. And so I’m very glad that I did because she’s she’s been incredible. And as you mentioned, she created this, very important advisory regarding leaves because, as I mentioned at the very, very beginning of this call, like this advice can change. And so we wanted to get this memo out to let people know that if you are doing that, essentially you are going to be aerosolizing those chemicals and not just the chemicals that were, probably already settled on the leaves, but an unpredictable mix of new chemicals as well.

I can’t remember the exact number of cars, but it derailed in East Palestine, which is about a mile from the Pennsylvania line in eastern Ohio, and and it it exploded.
